blocks.title: What ICAI's published papers tell us
bullets: ICAI has not published examiners' comments for Paper 6, so this guidance comes from ICAI's suggested answers, RTPs and MTPs.

This is the **heaviest SM chapter in the paper**: 91 official items in the period reviewed — 21 past-paper items, 17 RTP descriptive questions, 17 RTP MCQ items, 29 MTP descriptive questions and 7 MTP case-MCQ items. Every attempt from May 2024 to May 2026 carries 7–12 marks from it.
Top areas by volume: **Porter's Five Forces** (17 items), **Competitive Landscape and strategic group mapping** (16), **PESTLE** (10), **Value Chain Analysis** (8), **Product Life Cycle** (7).

**ICAI's RTPs print their own chapter headings.** Every RTP from May 2024 to September 2026 places exactly two questions under 'Chapter 2-Strategic Analysis: External Environment' — always numbered 9 and 10. Question 9 is a case; question 10 is a direct theory question. One further strategic-group-mapping question, RTP May 2026 Q11, is printed under ICAI's Chapter 3 label but answered as a tool of industry environment analysis, so it is placed here.

Four headings have never carried a question of their own in the period reviewed: §2.1 Introduction, §2.5.4 Value Creation, §2.6 Market & Customer and §2.6.1 Customer. They are still written up in full here and carry chapter-test questions, because the 2026 syllabus edition added them.

blocks.title: How ICAI answers this chapter (study guidance)
bullets: Case questions carry an **identification mark**: name the tool or force first (Strategic Group Mapping, PESTLE, Threat of New Entrants, Demographic Environment), then reproduce the study-material list, then apply it to the facts. ICAI's own answers follow exactly that order.

ICAI's answers are **list-faithful**: five steps to understand the competitive landscape, six PESTLE factors, seven barriers to entry, six conditions of cut-throat rivalry, five primary and four support activities, five characteristics of business products, four steps in international strategic planning, four steps in strategic group mapping.

Two questions recur almost verbatim across papers. 'Value chain analysis… support activities' appears as PYQ May 2025 Q7(a) and MTP Jan 2026 S1 Q4(a) word for word; 'both activities are intertwined… primary activities' appears as PYQ Sep 2024 Q6(b), RTP Sep 2025 Q10 and RTP Sep 2026 Q10. Learn both halves of the value chain.

Where a case names rival **groups** (price bands, segments, feature tiers), ICAI's answer is **strategic group mapping** with its four-step procedure — never SWOT and never the BCG matrix. This single answer covers PYQ Jan 2025 MCQ 10, PYQ Jan 2026 Q5(a), MTP Mar 2024 S1 Q3(a), MTP Sep 2024 S2 Q4(b) OR, MTP May 2026 S1 Q1(a), MTP Sep 2026 S2 Q2(b), RTP May 2025 MCQ 4, RTP Jan 2026 MCQ 5 and RTP Sep 2026 MCQ 4.

blocks.title: Where candidates lose marks here
bullets: Answering a 'competitive landscape' case with Porter's Five Forces. ICAI's answer to the Riya Sharma confectionery case (RTP May 2024 Q9, repeated in RTP Jan 2026 Q9) is the **five steps to understand the competitive landscape**, even though the stem talks about market dynamics and rising competition.

Mixing the **Demographic** and **Socio-cultural** environments. ICAI's test: age, gender, income, education, assets, region are *characteristics* of the population — demographic. Traditions, values, beliefs, literacy standards, ethics, stratification are *behaviour and belief* — socio-cultural.

Writing PESTLE's 'S' as 'social' only. The study material heads it **socio-cultural**, and the drivers table lists lifestyle trends, demographics, consumer attitudes, buying patterns, ethnic/religious factors and media perception under it.

Listing primary activities when the question asks for support activities, or the reverse. Primary: inbound logistics, operations, outbound logistics, marketing and sales, service. Support: procurement, technology development, human resource management, infrastructure.

concepts.title: 2.1–2.2.1 Introduction; Strategic Analysis; Issues to Consider
understand: **Introduction (§2.1).** Organisations range from small local businesses to multinational corporations and are distinguished by size, type of products, markets, geographical coverage and legal status. Whatever the distinguishing feature, ==they do not operate in a vacuum==: they continuously act and react to what happens outside their periphery. The factors outside business operations are the **organisational or business environment** — in the specific context of business, **a set of all external factors that weigh in the minds of the managers**. Drawing an analogy with 'atmosphere', one can envision **layers** of such influences: international politico-legal, socio-cultural, economic, demographic, ecological and technological environment → the same domestic layer → industry-shaping competitive forces → the firm's stakeholders → the firm's internal environment.

The process of strategy formulation **begins with a strategic analysis**, whose objective is to compile information about internal and external environments in order to assess possibilities while formulating strategic objectives and contemplating strategic activities.

**Strategic analysis (§2.2).** Strategy formulation is not a task in which managers can get by with intuition, opinions, instincts and creative thinking. ==Judgments about what strategies to pursue need to flow directly from analysis of a firm's external environment and its internal resources and capabilities.==

**Environmental scanning** is a natural and continuous activity for every business: some do it informally, others have a formal structure. It is just as important to learn about a change in tax regulations through television news as through well-established reading material from experts — **the capacity to collect important information in informal settings usually separates great entrepreneurs and managers**. But using *only* informal techniques exposes the organisation to **missed opportunities and unanticipated hazards**; a systematic approach is essential for managing risk and uncertainty.

**The two important situational considerations** are: (1) **industry and competitive conditions**, and (2) **an organisation's own capabilities, resources, internal strengths, weaknesses and market position**.

**The analytical sequence** runs from strategic appraisal of the external and internal situation → evaluation of alternative strategies → the final choice of strategy. Without perceptive understanding of both environments, managers are far more likely to finalise a game plan that does not fit the situation, holds little prospect of competitive advantage and is unlikely to boost performance.

==**Two major limitations of strategic analysis.** First, it gives a lot of innovative options but does not tell which one to pick — the options can be overlapping, confusing or difficult to implement. Second, it can be time-consuming, hurting overall organisational functioning and straining other efficient innovations such as developing a new product or service.==

**Issues to consider (§2.2.1) — three of them.** **(i) Strategy evolves over a period of time.** Each strategic decision must balance the different factors that impact and constrain strategy; a key element of strategic analysis is the probable outcomes of everyday decisions. A current strategy is the result of several little choices taken over a protracted period. Management radically changes strategy when it tries to speed up organisational growth. Strategy is influenced by experience but has to be updated when results become clear — it therefore **evolves with time**.

**(ii) Balance of external and internal factors.** In practice, strategic analysis necessitates a reasonable balance between many and conflicting challenges, because **a perfect fit between them is unlikely**. Management must consider opportunities, influences and constraints together: there are factors *driving* a decision, such as entering a new market, and concurrently *constraints* that limit the option, such as the presence of a large opponent. Some of these aspects are under the firm's control; others are way beyond existing capabilities.

**(iii) Risk.** The complexity and intermingling of variables in the environment reduces strategic balance. Competitive markets, liberalisation, globalisation, booms, recessions, technological advancements and inter-country relationships all pose risk at varying degrees. An important task is to **identify potential imbalances or risks and assess their consequences**.

**External risk** arises from inconsistencies between strategies and the forces in the environment. **Internal risk** arises from forces that are either within the organisation or directly interacting with it on a routine basis.

**The framework of strategic analysis.** External analysis has four components — **Customer Analysis** (segments, motivations, unmet needs), **Competitor Analysis** (strategic groups, performance, objectives, strategies, culture, cost structure), **Market Analysis** (size, growth, profitability, entry barriers) and **Environmental Analysis** (technological, government, economic, cultural, demographic). Internal analysis has two — **Performance Analysis** (profitability, sales, customer satisfaction, product quality, relative cost, new products, human resources) and **Determinants Analysis** (past and current strategies, strategic problems, organisational capabilities and constraints, financial resources, strengths and weaknesses). External analysis yields opportunities, threats, trends and strategic uncertainties; internal analysis yields strategic strengths, weaknesses, problems, constraints and uncertainties. Both feed **strategy identification and selection**: identify strategic alternatives → select strategy → implement the operating plan → review strategies.

**Industries differ widely** in economic characteristics, competitive situations and future profit prospects — by overall size and market growth rate, pace of technological change, geographic boundaries, number and size of buyers and sellers, whether products are virtually identical or highly differentiated, the extent to which costs are affected by economies of scale, distribution channels, marketing opportunities, disposable income of prospective buyers and government support. Competition focuses on **price** in some industries, on **quality and reliability** in others (monitors for PCs and laptops), on **product features and performance** (mobile phones), on **quick service and convenience** (online shopping and fast foods) or on **brand reputation** (laundry detergents and soft drinks). ==Leading companies in unattractive industries can find it hard to earn respectable profits, while even weak companies in attractive industries can achieve good performance.==
concepts.example: A hospital chain studying the age profile of a city, the number and size of rival hospitals, insurance reimbursement rates and its own bed occupancy is doing all four kinds of external analysis at once — customer, competitor, market and environmental. If it then produces fifteen possible strategies and spends six months choosing between them, it has run straight into both published limitations of strategic analysis.

concepts.title: 2.3–2.3.1 Strategy and Business Environment; Micro and Macro Environment
understand: **Strategy and business environment (§2.3).** To accomplish the goals and objectives of a business, the strategist creates strategies and formulates policies considering **both internal and external factors**. Strategic management provides a framework for adjusting to the demands of an **unpredictable environment and an uncertain future**. The relationship is a triangle: **Management ↔ Strategy ↔ Environment ↔ Resources**.

==**The term 'business environment' refers to all external factors, influences or situations that in some way affect business decisions, plans and operations.**== It is **highly dynamic and continuously evolving**. Strategists provide an **interface** between organisational abilities and the opportunities and challenges of the larger environment. ==Organisational success is determined by its business environment, and even more from its relationship with it.==
**The five benefits of close and continuous interaction between a business and its environment** — the single most-asked list in this chapter:

**(i) Determine opportunities and threats.** The interaction explains opportunities and threats: it helps find new needs and wants of consumers, changes in laws, changes in social behaviours, and tells what new products competitors are bringing to market to attract consumers.

**(ii) Give direction for growth.** Interaction enables the business to identify areas for growth and expansion. Once the business is aware of and understands the changes happening around it, it can plan and strategise to have a successful business.
**(iii) Continuous learning.** Managers are motivated to continuously update their **knowledge, understanding and skills** to meet the predicted changes in the realm of business.

**(iv) Image building.** Environmental understanding helps organisations improve their image by showing **sensitivity to the environment** in which they operate. ICAI's own illustration: in view of the shortage of power, many companies set up **captive power plants** at their factories to meet their own requirement and extend surplus capacity in the vicinity.
**(v) Meeting competition.** It helps businesses analyse competitors' strategies and formulate their own accordingly — the idea is to flourish and beat competition for its products and services.

As the world gets smaller and competition increases, organisations face increasing pressure to develop their businesses and strengthen competitiveness. To flourish, ==a business must be aware of, assess and respond to the many opportunities and threats present in its environment==, and must be able to **handle and adapt** to them.

**Micro and macro environment (§2.3.1).** The environment can be described in terms of **opportunities and threats** in the external environment and **strengths and weaknesses** in the internal environment. The external environment is categorised into two major types: **micro environment** and **macro environment**.

==**Micro environment** is related to the small area or immediate periphery of an organisation. It influences the organisation **regularly and directly**. It consists of **suppliers, consumers, marketing intermediaries, competitors**, etc. — specific to the said business or firm.== Within the micro environment, a firm must address: the **employees** of the firm, their characteristics and how they are organised; the existing **customer base** on which the firm relies for business; the ways in which the firm can raise its **finance**; who the firm's **suppliers** are and how the links between the two are being developed; the local **community** within which the firm operates; and the **direct competition** and their comparative performance.

==**The macro environment** is the portion of the outside world that significantly affects how an organisation operates but is typically much **beyond its direct control and influence**.== The factors in the micro environment often relate an organisation to the macro issues influencing the way a firm reacts in the marketplace.
concepts.example: A packaged-foods firm notices (a) a wholesaler demanding longer credit — micro, and (b) a nationwide shift towards low-sugar diets — macro. It can renegotiate the credit term; it cannot reverse the diet shift, only respond to it with a sugar-free line. That asymmetry is exactly what 'beyond its direct control and influence' means.

expected_questions.question: Distinguish between the micro and the macro environment of a business, and state the issues a firm must address within its micro environment.
answer_points: **Micro environment** relates to the small area or immediate periphery of the organisation and influences it regularly and directly; it consists of suppliers, consumers, marketing intermediaries and competitors, and is specific to the particular firm.

**Macro environment** is the portion of the outside world that significantly affects how an organisation operates but is typically much beyond its direct control and influence; it has broader dimensions — economic, socio-cultural, technological, political and legal factors.

**Issues within the micro environment:** the employees of the firm, their characteristics and how they are organised; the existing customer base on which the firm relies; the ways in which the firm can raise its finance; who the firm's suppliers are and how the links between the two are developed; the local community within which the firm operates; and the direct competition and their comparative performance.
The factors in the micro environment often relate an organisation to the macro issues influencing the way it reacts in the marketplace.
Both are **external**; the internal environment is a separate matter of strengths and weaknesses.

official_questions.question: Yash is planning to launch his new tech start-up. He is exploring different locations across the country to establish his company in the right business environment. One option is the city of Bengaluru, the silicon valley of India, with an engaging network of entrepreneurs, investors, advisors and mentors. Coupled with various subsidies for new ventures and tax benefits, Bengaluru might be an ideal choice for Yash to establish his company and increase the chances of success. Define the term Business Environment with respect to the above scenario. Explain the different ways in which the interaction of a business with its environment can be helpful in developing a successful strategy. (1 + 4 = 5 Marks)
answer_points: **Business Environment** refers to all external factors, influences or situations that affect business decisions, plans and operations. In Yash's case these factors include the dynamic and evolving conditions in Bengaluru, which impact the strategic decisions for his tech start-up.

**Determine Opportunities and Threats:** interaction helps Yash identify new consumer needs, emerging trends and potential market opportunities, guiding the development of innovative products and services; understanding changes in laws, social behaviours and competitor actions enables him to anticipate and mitigate threats, keeping the start-up resilient and adaptive.

**Give Direction for Growth:** by analysing the external environment Yash can pinpoint areas for expansion; recognising market trends and technological advancements allows him to strategise so the start-up scales successfully, aligning its goals with market dynamics.

**Continuous Learning:** continuous interaction motivates Yash and his team to update their knowledge, understanding and skills; staying informed about industry trends keeps the start-up competitive and promotes innovation and responsiveness.

**Image Building:** understanding and responding to environmental needs helps build a positive image — adopting sustainable practices or contributing to local initiatives enhances reputation and attracts customers and partners who value corporate social responsibility.

**Meeting Competition:** interaction allows Yash to analyse competitors' strategies and adapt; understanding their strengths and weaknesses helps craft strategies that provide a competitive edge and position the start-up uniquely in the market.

concepts.title: 2.3.2 Elements of the Macro Environment
understand: **The macro environment has broader dimensions**: it consists of **economic, socio-cultural, technological, political and legal** factors. Classifying the relevant environment into components or sectors helps an organisation **cope with its complexity, comprehend the different influences operating, and relate the environmental changes to its strategic management process**.

ICAI quotes **Gluek and Jauch**: "The environment includes factors outside the firm which can lead to opportunities for, or threats to the firm. Although, there are many factors, the most important of the factors are **socio-economic, technological, supplier, competitors, and government**."

**1. Demographic Environment.** Demographics are the characteristics of a population that have been classified and explained according to certain criteria such as **age, gender and income**, in order to understand the features of a specific group. Demographical analysis considers **race, age, income, education, possession of assets, house ownership, job position, region, and the degree of education**. India has a relatively younger population compared with many other countries, and many multinationals are interested in India considering its population size. Two issues must be addressed: ==**What demographic trends will affect the market size of the industry? What demographic trends represent opportunities or threats?**== The **size, age distribution, geographic dispersion, ethnic mix and income distribution** of a population are all of great importance.

**2. Socio-Cultural Environment.** A general factor that influences almost all enterprises in a similar manner. It represents a complex group of factors such as **social traditions, values and beliefs, level and standards of literacy, the ethical standards and state of society, the extent of social stratification, conflict and cohesiveness**. ==It differs from demographics in the sense that it is **not the characteristics of the population, but the behaviour and the belief system** of that population.== The **core beliefs of a particular society tend to be persistent** — it is difficult for a business to change these core values, so businesses have to adjust to social norms and beliefs to operate successfully. The social environment primarily affects the strategic management process in the areas of **mission and objective setting, and decisions related to products and markets**.

**3. Economic Environment.** Economic conditions have a **direct bearing** on business strategies. The economic environment refers to the overall economic situation around the business and includes conditions at the **regional, national and global** levels; it encompasses conditions in the markets for resources that affect the supply of inputs and outputs, their costs, and the dependability, quality and availability. ==Economic environment determines the **strength and size of the market**.== Purchasing power depends on **current income, prices, savings, circulation of money, debt and credit availability**; the **income distribution pattern** determines business possibilities. The factors include **gross domestic product, per capita income, markets for goods and services, availability of capital, foreign exchange reserve, growth of foreign trade, strength of capital market, interest rates, disposable income, unemployment and inflation**. ICAI's illustration: **higher interest rates are detrimental for businesses with high debt**; in the real estate market they reduce prospective buyers' ability to avail loans and pay instalments, thus lowering demand.

**4. Political-Legal Environment.** Takes into account the **general level of political development, the degree to which business and economic issues have been politicised, the degree of political morality, the state of law and order, political stability, the political ideology and practices of the ruling party, the effectiveness and purposefulness of governmental agencies, and the scope and type of governmental intervention** in the economy and industry. It is **partly general to all similar enterprises and partly specific to an individual enterprise**. Businesses prefer a country with a sound legal system, and must have a good working knowledge of the major laws protecting **consumers, competition and organizations** — companies, competition, intellectual property, foreign exchange and labour law. **Nationalism** supports measures aimed at enhancing a country's position in international business: ICAI names **Make in India**, **Aatmanirbhar Bharat** and the **Production Linked Incentives scheme**, which rewards businesses for increased sales of goods produced domestically, encourages foreign businesses to open in India, incentivises domestic manufacturing expansion, creates jobs and lessens India's reliance on imports.

**5. Technological Environment.** Technology has changed the way people communicate and do things, and the way businesses operate. ==**Technology and business are linked and are interdependent on one another.**== Businesses help society access the outcomes of technological research and development, raising everyone's standard of living. With technology, organisations **reduce paperwork, schedule payments more efficiently and coordinate inventories effectively**, which reduces costs and **shrinks time and distance**, capturing competitive advantage. Technological advancements might require a business to **drastically alter its operational, production and marketing strategies**. ==Technology is leading to many new business opportunities **as well as making obsolete most of the existing business products and services** — it can act as an opportunity when effectively adopted, and as a threat at the same time.== ICAI names **artificial intelligence, machine learning and robotic process automation** as new tools that can be both.

concepts.title: 2.3.3 PESTLE — A Tool to Analyse the Macro Environment
understand: **PESTLE** is the framework for analysis of macro-environmental factors, frequently used to assess the business environment in which a firm operates. It was formerly **PEST** — political, economic, social and technological — and was ==later **expanded to include environmental and legal factors**==.

PESTLE analysis involves **identifying the political, economic, socio-cultural, technological, legal and environmental influences** on an organisation and providing **a way of scanning the environmental influences that have affected or are likely to affect an organisation or its policy**.
The acronym: **P – political · E – economic · S – socio-cultural · T – technological · L – legal · E – environmental**.
==**The advantage of this tool is that it encourages management into proactive and structured thinking in its decision making.**== It is also **simple to understand and quick to implement**.
**The Key Factors — six, in the study material's own words:**

**Political factors** are how and to what extent the **government intervenes in the economy and the activities of business firms**. They may also influence the goods and services which the government wants to be provided and those it does not. Governments have great influence on the **health, education and infrastructure** of a nation.

**Economic factors** have major impacts on how businesses operate and take decisions. **Interest rates** affect a firm's cost of capital and therefore the extent to which a business grows and expands. **Exchange rates** affect the costs of exporting goods and the supply and price of imported goods. **Money supply, inflation, credit flow, per capita income and growth rates** all bear on business decisions.
**Social factors** affect the **demand** for a company's products and **how that company operates**.

**Technological factors** can determine **barriers to entry**, the **minimum efficient production level** and influence **outsourcing decisions**; technological shifts can affect **costs, quality, and lead to innovation**.
**Legal factors** affect **how a company operates, its costs, and the demand for its products, ease of business**.

**Environmental factors** affect industries such as **tourism, farming and insurance**. Growing awareness of climate change is affecting how companies operate and the products they offer — ==**it is both creating new markets and diminishing or destroying existing ones**==.

**The drivers of change.** On the basis of these factors it should be possible to identify a number of key environmental influences, which are in effect the **drivers of change** — the factors that require to be considered in making meaningful decisions. The study material's table lists, under each head: **Political** — political stability; political principles and ideologies; current and future taxation policy; regulatory bodies and processes; government policies; government term and change; thrust areas of political leaders. **Economic** — economy situation and trends; market and trade cycles; specific industry factors; customer/end-user drivers; interest and exchange rates; inflation and unemployment; strength of consumer spending. **Social** — lifestyle trends; demographics; consumer attitudes and opinions; brand, company, technology image; consumer buying patterns; ethnic/religious factors; media views and perception. **Technological** — replacement technology/solutions; maturity of technology; manufacturing maturity and capacity; innovation potential; technology access, licensing, patents, property rights and copyrights. **Legal** — business and corporate laws; employment law; competition law; health and safety law; international treaty and law; regional legislation. **Environmental** — ecological/environmental issues; environmental hazards; environmental legislation; energy consumption; waste disposal.

That is ICAI's own answer to the ABC Corp question, asked four times.

expected_questions.question: What is PESTLE analysis? State its advantage, and explain the six key factors it covers.
answer_points: PESTLE is a framework for the analysis of macro-environmental factors. It involves identifying the political, economic, socio-cultural, technological, legal and environmental influences on an organisation and provides a way of scanning the environmental influences that have affected or are likely to affect an organisation or its policy. It was earlier PEST and was later expanded to include environmental and legal factors.
**Advantage:** it is simple to understand and quick to implement, and it encourages management into proactive and structured thinking in its decision making.

**Political** — how and to what extent the government intervenes in the economy and in business activity; influence over which goods and services are provided; great influence on health, education and infrastructure.

**Economic** — interest rates affect the cost of capital and therefore growth and expansion; exchange rates affect export costs and the supply and price of imports; money supply, inflation, credit flow, per capita income and growth rates all bear on decisions.

**Socio-cultural** — affects the demand for a company's products and how the company operates. **Technological** — determines barriers to entry and the minimum efficient production level, influences outsourcing decisions, and affects costs, quality and innovation.

**Legal** — affects how a company operates, its costs, the demand for its products and the ease of doing business. **Environmental** — affects industries such as tourism, farming and insurance; growing climate-change awareness is both creating new markets and diminishing or destroying existing ones.
keywords: creating new markets and destroying existing ones

expected_questions.question: Identify the key environmental influences — the 'drivers of change' — that the study material lists under the Political and the Technological heads of a PESTLE analysis.
answer_points: **Political drivers of change:** political stability; political principles and ideologies; current and future taxation policy; regulatory bodies and processes; government policies; government term and change; thrust areas of political leaders.

**Technological drivers of change:** replacement technology and solutions; maturity of technology; manufacturing maturity and capacity; innovation potential; technology access, licensing, patents, property rights and copyrights.
These drivers are the factors that require to be considered in making meaningful decisions — the practical output of a PESTLE scan.

The remaining four heads carry their own driver lists: economic (economy situation and trends, market and trade cycles, specific industry factors, customer drivers, interest and exchange rates, inflation and unemployment, strength of consumer spending); social (lifestyle trends, demographics, consumer attitudes and opinions, brand and technology image, consumer buying patterns, ethnic/religious factors, media views and perception); legal (business and corporate laws, employment law, competition law, health and safety law, international treaty and law, regional legislation); environmental (ecological issues, environmental hazards, environmental legislation, energy consumption, waste disposal).
keywords: licensing, patents, property rights and copyrights

official_questions.question: How does the PESTLE framework assist in analyzing the macro-environment?
answer_points: The PESTLE framework assists in analysing the macro-environment by **systematically evaluating six external factors** that impact an organisation's operations and strategy.
**1. Political Factors:** government policies, regulations, political stability and taxation. Understanding these helps organisations anticipate regulatory changes and government interventions.
**2. Economic Factors:** interest rates, inflation, exchange rates and economic growth, which influence business costs, consumer purchasing power and overall market conditions.
**3. Social Factors:** demographic trends, lifestyle changes, cultural norms and consumer attitudes; insights help align products and services with evolving consumer preferences.
**4. Technological Factors:** technological advancements, innovation rates and technological infrastructure, which impact production processes, product development and competitive positioning.

**5. Legal Factors:** business laws, employment regulations, health and safety standards and compliance requirements — crucial for regulatory compliance and avoiding legal risks. **6. Environmental Factors:** ecological issues, sustainability practices and environmental regulations; awareness helps businesses adapt to climate change and meet sustainability goals.

**Closing line (ICAI's own):** by analysing these factors the PESTLE framework provides a comprehensive understanding of the macro-environment, helping organisations anticipate changes, adapt strategies and make informed decisions.
also_asked_as: MTP-S24-S2-SQ4b asks the identical question and ICAI's answer is reproduced word for word; that MTP also offers an 'OR' alternative on strategic group mapping, which is covered at S02.23.

official_questions.question: ABC Corp, a multinational consumer electronics company, is planning to expand its operations into a new country. The company's senior management is evaluating the potential risks and opportunities of entering this new market. As part of their analysis, they decide to use the PESTLE framework to assess the external factors that could impact their decision. How can the PESTLE framework help ABC Corp assess the external factors affecting its decision to expand into a new country? (5 Marks)
answer_points: **Political Factors:** stability of the government, government policies on foreign investment, trade agreements and regulatory frameworks — allowing ABC Corp to assess the political risks of entering the new market.
**Economic Factors:** GDP growth rate, inflation rate, exchange rates and economic stability — letting the company understand the economic environment and its potential impact on business operations.
**Social Factors:** cultural norms, demographics and lifestyle trends, which influence consumer behaviour and demand; understanding them helps tailor marketing strategies to the new market.
**Technological Factors:** infrastructure, technological advancements and the level of technology adoption, which determine the technological requirements for entering the market.
**Legal Factors:** laws and regulations on foreign investment, intellectual property rights and labour, ensuring compliance with legal requirements.

**Environmental Factors:** climate change, environmental regulations and sustainability practices, which affect operations and reputation. Overall, PESTLE gives ABC Corp a comprehensive analysis of the external factors affecting the expansion decision, helping it make informed and strategic decisions.
also_asked_as: The same ABC Corp question appears twice more with an identical published answer: MTP-M24-S1-SQ1b and MTP-S25-S2-SQ1a. Three appearances in fifteen MTPs make this the single most repeated PESTLE question in the paper.

concepts.title: 2.3.4–2.3.5 Internationalization of Business; International Environment
understand: **Internationalisation (§2.3.4)** has emerged as the **dominant commercial trend over the last couple of decades**. It enables a business to **enter new markets in search of greater earnings and less expensive resources**, to **achieve greater economies of scale** and to **extend the lifespan of its products**.

==The strategic-management process is **essentially the same** for global firms as for domestic firms; nevertheless, international processes are **much more complicated due to additional variables and linkages**.== Scanning the external environment is one method for an organisation to identify opportunities and threats in global markets.

**Three characteristics of a global business.** (i) It is a **conglomerate of multiple units** located in different parts of the globe but all **linked by common ownership**. (ii) Multiple units **draw on a common pool of resources** — money, credit, information, patents, trade names and control systems. (iii) The units **respond to some common strategy**; besides, its managers and shareholders are also based in different nations.

**Developing internationally — the four steps in international strategic planning.** ==International development is expensive and challenging, so moving on in a thorough and structured manner is the ideal approach.== (1) **Evaluate global opportunities and threats** and rate them with the internal capabilities. (2) **Describe the scope** of the firm's global commercial operations. (3) **Create the firm's global business objectives.** (4) **Develop distinct corporate strategies** for the global business and the whole organisation.

**Why do businesses go global?** Two important factors in the rapid rise of multinationals are **technological developments and evolving political views**: worldwide communication makes it easier to define and implement global strategy by linking headquarters with overseas operations, and improved transportation has increased the mobility of money, people, raw materials and finished items. The reasons are:
**(i) The need to grow** — the first and foremost reason, and the basic need of every organisation; finding opportunities elsewhere, organisations extend and globalise their operations.
**(ii) Shrinking time and distance** — faster communication, speedier transportation, growing financial flow of funds and rapid technological changes.
**(iii) Domestic markets are no longer adequate** — the competition present domestically may not exist in some international markets.
**(iv) Need for reliable or cheaper sources** of raw materials, cheap labour; many foreign businesses shift operations to take advantage of a vast pool of talent.
**(v) Reducing high transportation costs** — it may be cheaper to produce near the market.
**(vi) Foreign markets opening up or growing big** — exporters then look at overseas manufacturing plants and sales branches to generate higher sales and better cash flow.

**(vii) The rise of services** to constitute the largest single sector in the world economy, and **regional economic integration** involving both the world's largest economies and certain developing economies.

**(viii) The apparent and real collapse of international trade barriers**, which redefines the roles of state and industry: increased privatisation of manufacturing and services, less government interference, more dependence on the value-added sector, and lower trade tariffs and customs barriers.

**(ix) Strategic alliances** — globalisation has made companies in different countries form alliances to ward off economic and technological threats and leverage their respective comparative and competitive advantages.

**International environment (§2.3.5).** The social, cultural, demographic, environmental, political, governmental, legal and technological factors an international organisation faces are **nearly limitless**, and their number and complexity **increase manifold** as the number of products and geographic areas served increase. ==An assessment of the external environment is the **first step toward internationalisation**.== Assessments can be done at **three levels: multinational, regional and country**.

**Multinational environmental analysis** involves **identifying, anticipating and monitoring significant components of the global environment on a large scale**. Understanding global developments covering economic and other macro elements is important; governments may have **free or interventionist tendencies** that must be carefully considered, and these characteristics are evaluated on their **present and expected future impact**.

**Regional environmental analysis** is a **more in-depth evaluation of the critical factors in a specific geographical area**, emphasising the discovery of market opportunities for goods, services or innovations in the chosen location.

**Country environmental analysis** takes a **deeper look** at the important environmental factors; study of **economic, legal, political and cultural dimensions** is required for planning to succeed, and the analysis must be **customised for each country** to develop effective market-entrance strategies.

International environment has become an inherent part of strategic management for businesses of all sizes with global interests, involving **political risks, cultural differences, exchange rate fluctuations, legal compliances and taxation issues**.
concepts.example: An Indian pharmaceutical firm scans world regulatory trends and currency blocs (multinational level), then narrows to the East African market for generics (regional level), then studies Kenya's drug-pricing law, tax regime, political stability and prescribing culture before choosing between export and a local plant (country level). Each level is narrower and deeper than the last.

official_questions.question: "International development is expensive and challenging". In the context of the statement, explain the internationalization of business and the steps involved in such strategic planning. (5 Marks)
answer_points: **Internationalization has become a pivotal trend** for businesses aiming to enhance profitability and access cheaper resources. It allows companies to explore new markets, achieve economies of scale and prolong product lifecycles. However, the process is **complex due to additional variables and linkages** that differ from domestic operations.
**Step 1 — Evaluate Global Opportunities and Threats:** businesses must assess potential global markets, identifying opportunities and threats while aligning them with their internal capabilities.
**Step 2 — Describe the Scope of Operations:** clearly defining the extent of the firm's international commercial activities is crucial for focused strategy development.
**Step 3 — Create Global Business Objectives:** establishing clear objectives guides the organisation's international efforts and aligns with its overall mission.
**Step 4 — Develop Distinct Corporate Strategies:** formulating specific strategies tailored for global operations ensures the organisation can effectively compete in diverse markets.

These steps facilitate the identification of market opportunities and the formulation of effective global strategies, enabling businesses to thrive in the international arena **despite the inherent challenges and costs** associated with such expansion.

official_questions.question: "Beyond the basic need to grow modern organizations are driven by a mix of market inadequacy resource needs and the collapse of international barriers." Analyse the various reasons why companies choose to globalise their operations. (5 Marks)
answer_points: Globalisation refers to the process of expanding business operations beyond domestic boundaries into international markets, for strategic, economic and competitive reasons.
**1. Need for Growth** — the foremost reason for internationalisation; organisations expand globally in search of new business opportunities, higher sales and greater earnings.
**2. Shrinking Time and Distance** — rapid technological developments, faster communication, speedier transportation and increased financial flows have reduced geographical barriers.
**3. Inadequacy of Domestic Markets** — domestic markets are often insufficient for long-term growth; companies enter international markets where competition may be less intense.

**4. Availability of Resources** — access to reliable and cheaper raw materials, skilled labour and talent pools abroad. **5. Reduction in Transportation Costs** — overseas plants near target markets reduce transportation costs, delivery time and logistics expenses.

**6. Expansion of Foreign Markets** — when foreign markets grow substantially, organisations establish overseas production and sales units to increase sales volume and improve cash flows. **7. Growth of Service Sector and Regional Integration** — the growing importance of services and regional economic integration encourage international expansion.

concepts.title: 2.4 Understanding Product and Industry
understand: **Businesses sell products.** ==A product can be either a good or a service — it might be a physical good, a service, or an experience.== Business products have **five characteristics**, and this five-item list is what every question under this heading asks for.

**1. Products are either tangible or intangible.** A **tangible** product can be handled, seen and physically felt — a car, book, pen, table, mobile handset. An **intangible** product is not a physical good — telecom services, banking, insurance or repair services.

**2. Product has a price.** Businesses determine the cost of their products and charge a price for them. ==**The dynamics of supply and demand influence the market price**; the market price is the price at which **quantity provided equals quantity desired**.== The price that may be paid is determined by **the market, the quality, the marketing and the targeted group**. ==In the present competitive world **price is often given by the market and businesses have to work on costs to maintain profitability**== — on account of competition, businesses are **not able to fix market price by adding a profit margin on costs**; rather, they work on **reducing costs given the prevailing market price**.

**3. Products have certain features that deliver satisfaction.** A **product feature is a component of a product that satisfies a consumer need**. Features determine product pricing, and businesses **alter features during the development process to optimise the user experience**. Products should provide **value satisfaction** to the customers for whom they are meant. Features distinguish a product in terms of its **function, design, quality and experience**. ==A customer's **cumulative experience with a product from its purchase to the end of its useful life** is an important component of a product feature.==

**4. Product is pivotal for business.** ==The product is **at the centre of business around which all strategic activities revolve**.== The product **enables production, quality, sales, marketing, logistics and other business processes** — it is the **driving force behind business activities**.

**5. A product has a useful life.** Every product has a **usable life after which it must be replaced**, as well as a **life cycle after which it is to be reinvented or may cease to exist**. ICAI's illustration: **fixed line telephone instruments have largely been replaced by mobile phones.**

**Why industries differ.** The surrounding discussion in §2.2 and §2.4 makes the industry point that follows from the product point: industries differ widely in economic characteristics, competitive situations and future profit prospects, and the basis of competition itself differs — **price** in some industries, **quality and reliability** in others (monitors for PCs and laptops), **product features and performance** (mobile phones), **quick service and convenience** (online shopping and fast foods), or **brand reputation** (laundry detergents and soft drinks). Situating the product in its industry is therefore the first step of industry analysis.
concepts.example: An office-furniture maker undercut by online retailers cannot raise its price — the market gives the price. Its only levers are the five characteristics: use better materials and design (tangible), add free installation and extended warranty (intangible and service features), work on costs rather than margins (price), keep the product at the centre of every process (pivotal), and plan the reinvention of each line before its useful life runs out (life cycle). That is ICAI's own answer to the Reshuffle Corp question.

expected_questions.question: "In the present competitive world price is often given by the market." Explain this statement with reference to the characteristics of business products, and state what it implies for a firm's approach to costing.
answer_points: A product can be either a good or a service; one of its five characteristics is that **product has a price**. The dynamics of supply and demand influence the market price, which is the price at which quantity provided equals quantity desired.
The price that may be paid is determined by the market, the quality, the marketing and the targeted group — not by the seller alone.

**Implication for costing:** on account of competition, businesses are not able to fix the market price by adding a profit margin on costs. Instead they must **work on reducing the costs given the prevailing market price** in order to maintain profitability.

The other characteristics interact with this: features determine product pricing, and businesses alter features during development to optimise the user experience, so cost reduction must not destroy the function, design, quality and experience that deliver value satisfaction.

Because the product is pivotal — the centre around which all strategic activities revolve — cost control has to run through production, quality, sales, marketing and logistics together, and must be planned against the product's useful life and life cycle.

official_questions.question: What are the key characteristics of business products that contribute to the overall competitiveness and dynamics of the market? (5 Marks)
answer_points: Businesses sell products. A product can be either a good or a service — it might be a physical good or a service, an experience.

**1. Products are either tangible or intangible.** A tangible product can be handled, seen and physically felt — a car, book, pen, table, mobile handset. An intangible product is not a physical good — telecom services, banking, insurance or repair services.

**2. Product has a price.** Businesses determine the cost of their products and charge a price. The dynamics of supply and demand influence the market price; the market price is the price at which quantity provided equals quantity desired. The price that may be paid is determined by the market, the quality, the marketing and the targeted group. In the present competitive world price is often given by the market and businesses have to work on costs to maintain profitability.

**3. Products have certain features that deliver satisfaction.** A product feature is a component of a product that satisfies a consumer need; features determine product pricing, and businesses alter features during the development process to optimise the user experience. Features distinguish a product in terms of function, design, quality and experience, and the customer's cumulative experience from purchase to the end of useful life is an important component of a product feature.

**4. Product is pivotal for business.** The product is at the centre of business around which all strategic activities revolve; it enables production, quality, sales, marketing, logistics and other business processes, and is the driving force behind business activities.

**5. A product has a useful life.** Every product has a usable life after which it must be replaced, as well as a life cycle after which it is to be reinvented or may cease to exist — fixed line telephone instruments have largely been replaced by mobile phones.

official_questions.question: "In a modern competitive landscape, the interaction of supply and demand determines the price at which quantity provided equals to quantity desired." Analyse the inherent characteristics of business products that must be managed to maintain profitability under these market dynamics. (5 Marks)
answer_points: Business products possess certain inherent characteristics that businesses must manage effectively to maintain profitability in a competitive market where price is determined by the interaction of supply and demand.
**1. Products are Tangible or Intangible** — a car, mobile phone or table, or banking, insurance and telecom services; both types must be managed efficiently to satisfy customer requirements.

**2. Product has a Price** — determined by market forces of supply and demand, the market price being where quantity supplied equals quantity demanded. In the present competitive environment businesses often cannot fix prices by simply adding profit margins over cost; therefore firms need to **control and reduce costs** to maintain profitability.

**3. Products have Features that Deliver Satisfaction** — design, quality, function and customer experience provide value and satisfaction; businesses continuously improve features to optimise customer experience and differentiate from competitors.

**4. Product is Pivotal for Business** — the centre around which all strategic and operational activities revolve, including production, quality control, marketing, logistics and sales; the product acts as the driving force behind operations and profitability.

**5. Product has a Useful Life** — every product has a useful life and a product life cycle after which it may require replacement, reinvention or discontinuation; businesses must innovate and update products continuously to remain competitive and profitable.

**Product Centric Approach:** keep products at the centre of strategic activities, aligning all business processes from production to sales and marketing to customer needs and expectations.

**Product Life Cycle Management:** be aware of the life cycle of products and plan for reinvention or replacement accordingly, introducing new product lines or upgrading existing ones to keep up with changing preferences and trends.

concepts.title: 2.4.1 Product Life Cycle
understand: ==**The product life cycle (PLC) is an S-shaped curve which exhibits the relationship of sales with respect to time for a product that passes through the four successive stages of introduction, growth, maturity and decline.**== It is **an important concept in strategic choice** and **a useful concept for guiding strategic choice**. ==If **businesses are substituted for product**, the concept of PLC could work just as well.==

**Stage 1 — Introduction.** **Slow sales growth**, in which **competition is almost negligible**, **prices are relatively high**, and **markets are limited**. The growth in sales is at a lower rate **because of lack of awareness on the part of customers**.

**Stage 2 — Growth.** **Rapid market acceptance.** The **demand expands rapidly, prices fall, competition increases and the market expands**. The customer **has knowledge about the product and shows interest in purchasing it**.

**Stage 3 — Maturity.** There is a **slowdown in the growth rate**. **Competition gets tough and the market gets stabilised. Profit comes down because of stiff competition.** At this stage organisations have to **work for maintaining stability**.

**Stage 4 — Decline.** **Sharp downward drift in sales.** Sales and profits fall sharply **because some new product replaces the existing product**. A **combination of strategies** can be implemented to stay in the market, **either by diversification or retrenchment**.

==**The main advantage of the PLC approach is that it can be used to diagnose a portfolio of products (or businesses) in order to establish the stage at which each of them exists.**== Particular attention is to be paid to the businesses that are in the **declining** stage.

**The strategic choices that follow from the diagnosis:** **expansion** may be a feasible alternative for businesses in the **introductory and growth** stages; **mature** businesses may be used as **sources of cash for investment in other businesses which need resources**; a combination of strategies like **selective harvesting, retrenchment**, etc. may be adopted for **declining** businesses. In this way a **balanced portfolio of businesses** may be built up by exercising a strategic choice based on the PLC concept.
concepts.example: A logistics firm's road business is in maturity (stable market, thin margins) while its airways partnership is in decline (sales and profits down steeply) and its newly launched drone pilot is in introduction (high price, few customers, no rivals). The PLC diagnosis tells it to harvest road cash, retrench or diversify out of airways, and fund the drone venture — which is exactly the 'balanced portfolio' use the study material describes.

memory.trick: "I-G-M-D" ("Infants Grow, Mature, Decline") — and attach one price-and-competition fact to each: Introduction (high price, no competition), Growth (prices fall, competition rises), Maturity (tough competition, profit down), Decline (sales crash, replaced).
key: Introduction — slow growth, negligible competition, high prices, limited markets, no awareness
Growth — rapid acceptance, demand expands, prices fall, competition increases
Maturity — growth slows, competition tough, market stabilises, profit falls, maintain stability
Decline — sharp drift down, replaced by a new product, diversify or retrench

answer_points: The PLC is an **S-shaped curve** exhibiting the relationship of sales with respect to time for a product passing through four successive stages — introduction, growth, maturity and decline. If businesses are substituted for products, the concept works just as well.

**Introduction:** slow sales growth, almost negligible competition, relatively high prices and limited markets; growth is slow because of lack of customer awareness. **Growth:** rapid market acceptance — demand expands rapidly, prices fall, competition increases and the market expands.

**Maturity:** slowdown in the growth rate; competition gets tough, the market stabilises and profit comes down because of stiff competition, so organisations work for maintaining stability. **Decline:** sharp downward drift in sales as a new product replaces the existing one; a combination of strategies — diversification or retrenchment — may be used to stay in the market.

**Main advantage:** it can be used to **diagnose a portfolio of products (or businesses)** in order to establish the stage at which each exists, with particular attention to those in the declining stage.

official_questions.question: A company has recently launched a new product in the market. Initially, it faced slow sales growth, limited markets, and high prices. However, over time, the demand for the product expanded rapidly, prices fell, and competition increased. Identify the stages of the product life cycle (PLC) that the company went through.
answer_points: The company went through **two** stages of the product life cycle.

**Introduction stage:** initially the company faced slow sales growth, limited markets and high prices, which are characteristic of the introduction stage. During this stage **competition is almost negligible, and customers have limited knowledge about the product**.

**Growth stage:** over time the demand for the product expanded rapidly, prices fell and competition increased — typical features of the growth stage. In this stage **the product gains market acceptance, and customers become more aware of the product's benefits and show interest in purchasing it**.

concepts.title: 2.4.2 Value Chain Analysis
understand: **Why value matters.** With each transaction, successful businesses produce value for their consumers in the form of **satisfaction** and for themselves and their shareholders in the form of **profits**. ==Companies that generate more value are more likely to profit than those that generate less value.==

==**Value chain analysis is a method of examining each activity in the value chain of a business in order to identify areas for improvement.**== It is a method used by strategists to **break down each process that their business employs**, and can be used to improve the sequence of operations, enhancing efficiency and creating competitive advantage. It can be used by businesses of **all sizes, from sole proprietorships to multinational organisations**. When doing a value chain analysis you must analyse **how each stage in the process adds or subtracts value** from the end product or service.

**Origin.** Value chain analysis was **originally introduced as an accounting analysis** to shed light on the **'value added' of separate steps in complex manufacturing processes**, in order to determine where cost improvements could be made and/or value creation improved. ==The two basic steps of **identifying separate activities** and **assessing the value added from each** were linked to an analysis of an organisation's **competitive advantage by Michael Porter**.==

==**One of the key aspects of value chain analysis is the recognition that organizations are much more than a random collection of machines, material, money and people.** These resources are of no value unless **deployed into activities and organised into systems and routines** which ensure that products or services are produced which are valued by the final consumer/user.== It is these **competences to perform particular activities and the ability to manage linkages between activities** which are the source of competitive advantage. Porter argued that an understanding of strategic capability must start with an identification of these separate value activities.

**The five primary activities.** **(1) Inbound logistics** — activities concerned with **receiving, storing and distributing the inputs** to the product/service: materials handling, stock control, transport, warehousing. **(2) Operations** — **transform these inputs into the final product or service**: machining, packaging, assembly, testing — converting raw materials into finished goods. **(3) Outbound logistics** — **collect, store and distribute the product to customers**; for tangible products this means warehousing, materials handling and transport, and for services it may be more concerned with **arrangements for bringing customers to the service** if it is at a fixed location (e.g. sports events). **(4) Marketing and sales** — **the means whereby consumers/users are made aware of the product/service and are able to purchase it**: sales administration, advertising, selling; in public services, **communication networks which help users access a particular service**. **(5) Service** — all those activities which **enhance or maintain the value of a product/service**: installation, repair, training and spares.

**The four support activities.** Each group of primary activities is linked to support activities. **(1) Procurement** — the **processes for acquiring the various resource inputs to the primary activities (not the resources themselves)**; as such it occurs in **many parts of the organisation**. **(2) Technology development** — **all value activities have a 'technology', even if it is simply know-how**; the key technologies may concern the product directly (R&D, product design), the processes (process development) or a particular resource (raw-material improvements). **(3) Human resource management** — a particularly important area which **transcends all primary activities**: recruiting, managing, training, developing and rewarding people. **(4) Infrastructure** — the systems of **planning, finance, quality control and information management**, crucially important to performance in the primary activities; infrastructure also consists of **the structures and routines of the organisation which sustain its culture**.

==Primary and support activities are **intertwined**: this is the proposition ICAI puts to candidates three times, and the expected answer is 'Yes, I agree', followed by the definition and then whichever list the question asks for.==
concepts.example: A solar-panel maker that forms partnerships with retail chains to widen distribution is acting on **outbound logistics** — collecting, storing and distributing the product to customers. If instead it had negotiated better silicon contracts, that would be **procurement**; if it had improved cell efficiency in the lab, **technology development**; if it had set up an installation and repair network, **service**.

answer_points: Resources are **of no value unless deployed into activities and organised into systems and routines** which ensure that products or services are produced that are valued by the final consumer or user.

It is the **competences to perform particular activities** and the **ability to manage the linkages between activities** that are the source of competitive advantage for organisations; Porter argued that an understanding of strategic capability must start with an identification of these separate value activities.

official_questions.question: What do you mean by value chain analysis? Delineate the support activities in value chain analysis, as stated by Michael Porter. (1 + 4 = 5 Marks)
answer_points: **Value chain analysis** is a strategic tool used to examine each business activity to determine how it adds value, helping firms improve efficiency, identify cost-saving opportunities and gain competitive advantage through better coordination and performance of internal processes.
Michael Porter identified **four main categories of support activities** that support the primary activities and help the organisation achieve competitive advantage.

**1. Procurement:** the processes involved in acquiring the various resource inputs needed for the primary activities. It focuses on **how resources are sourced rather than the resources themselves**, and occurs across many parts of the organisation.

**2. Technology Development:** every value activity has an associated technology or know-how — R&D, product design, process development and improvements in resources such as raw materials. It enhances the efficiency and effectiveness of value activities.

concepts.title: 2.5 Industry Environment Analysis
understand: **A combination of ideas and methodologies** may be utilised to create a clear picture of **key industry traits, competition intensity, industry change drivers, rival firms' market positions and tactics, competitive success, and profit forecasts**. ==Industry analysis enables strategic understanding about the entire state of any industry and allows decisions about **whether the industry is lucrative or not**.==

==**The goal of the industry environment analysis, which is typically an important step of strategic analysis, is to estimate the amount of competitive pressures the business is presently facing and is expected to face in the near future.**==

**The analysis entails seeing the firm in the context of a bigger framework.** The purpose of industrial analysis is to **get insight into a wide range of elements within and outside the business**; analysing these elements **enhances knowledge of the surrounding and serves as the foundation for aligning strategy with changing industry circumstances and realities**.

Note the distinction from the macro environment: §2.3 covered what lies **outside the industry** and is beyond the firm's control; §2.5 covers the **industry** itself — the layer the chapter-opening figure calls the **industry-shaping competitive force**, sitting between the domestic macro environment and the firm's own stakeholders.

The chapter then supplies four tools for this layer, each with its own heading: **Porter's Five Forces Model** (§2.5.1) to diagnose competitive pressure, **Attractiveness of Industry** (§2.5.2) to draw the conclusion, the **Experience Curve** (§2.5.3) to explain cost positions within the industry, and **Value Creation** (§2.5.4) to explain where profit comes from.
concepts.example: A same-day delivery company planning to enter Tier-2 cities gathers four facts — e-commerce clients building in-house delivery, fuel prices up 18%, drone start-ups attracting venture capital, and large clients negotiating hard on rates. Industry environment analysis is the step of turning those four facts into an estimate of present and near-future competitive pressure; the Five Forces model is the framework that labels each one.

official_questions.question: SwiftDeliver Logistics Ltd. is a same-day delivery company operating in six metropolitan cities in India. The company is considering expanding to Tier-2 cities. As part of due diligence, the Strategic Planning team is conducting an industry environment analysis. The team has gathered the following information: (a) Many e-commerce firms are building in-house delivery capabilities. (b) Fuel prices have risen 18% in the past year. (c) Drone-based last-mile delivery start-ups are attracting significant venture capital funding. (d) Large e-commerce clients negotiate aggressively on delivery rates. Conduct a Porter's Five Forces analysis for SwiftDeliver using the information provided, identifying the relevant force for each bullet point.
answer_points: Porter's Five Forces Model, developed by Michael Porter, is a framework used to analyse the competitive forces operating in an industry and to assess its attractiveness.

**E-commerce firms building in-house delivery → Threat of New Entrants.** Large e-commerce companies developing their own logistics networks increase competition in the industry, reduce dependence on third-party logistics providers like SwiftDeliver and may adversely affect its market share.

**Fuel prices up 18% → Bargaining Power of Suppliers.** Fuel is a key input for logistics companies; an increase in fuel prices raises operating costs, indicating higher supplier bargaining power and affecting profitability.

**Drone-based last-mile start-ups attracting funding → Threat of Substitute Products or Services.** Drone delivery is an alternative mode of last-mile delivery; as the technology develops it may offer faster and more cost-effective solutions, posing a substitute threat to traditional logistics services.

**Large clients negotiating aggressively → Bargaining Power of Buyers.** Large customers place bulk orders and contribute significantly to revenue; their strong bargaining position enables them to demand lower prices, customised services and better delivery terms, reducing profit margins.

**Conclusion:** the industry analysis indicates a highly competitive environment characterised by increasing competition, strong bargaining power of buyers and suppliers, and emerging substitute technologies. Before expanding into Tier-2 cities, the company should focus on **improving operational efficiency, adopting innovative technologies, and differentiating its services** to sustain its competitive advantage.
