concepts.title: 2.5.1 Porter's Five Forces Model of Competition
understand: **Every business operates in a competitive environment,** and the competitive state of an industry applies a strong influence on how firms develop their strategies. ==**Porter's Five Forces analysis is a simple but efficient way for determining the key sources of competition in a business or industry** — a powerful and widely used tool to **systematically diagnose the significant competitive pressures in a market and assess the strength and importance of each**.== Understanding the variables that affect an industry helps to **adapt strategy, boost profitability, and stay ahead of the competition**. A strategist may use a strong position to organisational advantage, or reinforce a weak one to avoid making mistakes in future.

**Porter's unit of analysis.** Michael Porter believes that ==the basic unit of analysis for understanding is **a group of competitors producing goods or services that compete directly with each other**== — **it is the industry where competitive advantage is ultimately won or lost**. It is through competitive strategy that the organisation attempts to adopt an approach to compete in the industry. **The character, mix and intricacies of competitive forces are never the same from one industry to another.**

==**The five areas of the overall market** in which competitive pressures operate — the exact list ICAI asked for in January 2026:== **(i)** competitive pressures associated with the **market manoeuvring and jockeying for buyer patronage that goes on among rival sellers** in the industry; **(ii)** competitive pressures associated with the **threat of new entrants** into the market; **(iii)** competitive pressures coming from the **attempts of companies in other industries to win buyers over to their own substitute products**; **(iv)** competitive pressures stemming from **supplier bargaining power and supplier-seller collaboration**; **(v)** competitive pressures stemming from **buyer bargaining power and seller-buyer collaboration**.

**The three steps for using the model.** **Step 1:** identify the specific competitive pressures associated with each of the five forces. **Step 2:** evaluate **how strong** the pressures comprising each of the five forces are — **fierce, strong, moderate to normal, or weak**. **Step 3:** determine whether the **collective strength** of the five competitive forces is **conducive to earning attractive profits**.

Porter's model is ==**one of the most effective and enduring conceptual frameworks** used to assess the nature of the competitive environment and to describe an industry's structure. **The interrelationship among these five forces gives each industry its own particular competitive environment.**== By applying it to their own industries, managers can gauge their firm's strengths, weaknesses and future opportunities.

**FORCE I — The Threat of New Entrants.** ==New entrants **reduce industry profitability** because they **add new production capacity**, leading to an increase in supply of the product **even at a lower price**, and can **substantially erode existing firms' market share position**.== New entrants are always a powerful source of competition; the new capacity and product range they bring throw up new competitive pressure, and **the bigger the new entrant, the more severe the competitive effect**. New entrants also **place a limit on prices** and affect profitability. ==A firm's profitability tends to be **higher when other firms are blocked from entering** the industry.== To discourage new entrants, existing firms try to **raise barriers to entry** — **economic forces (or 'hurdles') that slow down or impede entry by other firms**.

**The seven barriers to entry.** **(i) Capital Requirements** — when a large amount of capital is required to enter an industry, firms lacking funds are **effectively barred**, enhancing the profitability of existing firms. **(ii) Economies of Scale** — the **decline in the per-unit cost of production (or other activity) as volume grows**; a large firm enjoying economies of scale can produce high volumes at successively lower costs, which discourages new entrants. **(iii) Product Differentiation** — the **physical or perceptual differences, or enhancements, that make a product special or unique in the eyes of customers** (ICAI's example: personal care products and cosmetics); differentiation reinforces entry barriers because **the cost of creating genuine product differences may be too high for new entrants**. **(iv) Switching Costs** — a new entrant must persuade existing customers of other companies to switch; to switch, buyers may need to **test a new firm's product, negotiate new purchase contracts, train personnel to use the equipment, or modify facilities**, incurring substantial **financial (and psychological)** costs, so when switching costs are high buyers are reluctant to change. **(v) Brand Identity** — particularly important for **infrequently purchased products that carry a high unit cost** to the buyer; new entrants face significant difficulty building brand identity because they must **commit substantial resources over a long period**. **(vi) Access to Distribution Channels** — the **unavailability of distribution channels** for new entrants; despite the growing power of the internet, many firms continue to rely on control of physical distribution channels, and existing firms often have significant influence over them and can **retard or impede their use** by new firms. **(vii) Possibility of Aggressive Retaliation** — sometimes **the mere threat** of aggressive retaliation deters entry; for example, a new firm's product introduction may lead incumbents to **reduce prices and increase advertising budgets**.

**FORCE II — Bargaining Power of Buyers.** This force becomes **heavier depending on the possibilities of the buyers forming groups or cartels** — mostly a phenomenon seen in **industrial products**, where users come together formally or informally and exert pressure on the producer. ==Buyer power influences **not only the prices the producer can charge but also, in many cases, the costs and investments of the producer**, because powerful buyers usually bargain for better services, which involve cost and investment on the producer's part.== The leverage is particularly evident when: **(i)** buyers have **full knowledge of the sources of products and their substitutes**; **(ii)** they **spend a lot of money on the industry's products, i.e. they are big buyers**; **(iii)** the industry's product is **not perceived as critical to the buyer's needs** and buyers are **more concentrated than the firms supplying** the product, so they can easily switch to available substitutes.

**FORCE III — Bargaining Power of Suppliers.** ==**The more specialised the offering from the supplier, the greater is his clout**; and if suppliers are also **limited in number**, they stand a still better chance of exhibiting bargaining power.== Supplier power **determines the cost of raw materials and other inputs** of the industry and therefore **industry attractiveness and profitability**. Suppliers command bargaining power when: **(i)** their products are **crucial to the buyer and substitutes are not available**; **(ii)** they can **erect high switching costs**; **(iii)** they are **more concentrated than their buyers**.

**FORCE IV — The Nature of Rivalry in the Industry.** This is what is normally understood as competition. For any player the competitors influence strategic decisions at different levels, and the impact is evident more at the **functional level** — in prices charged, advertising, pressures on costs and product. ==**The intensity of rivalry is a significant determinant of industry attractiveness and profitability**; it can influence the costs of suppliers, distribution and attracting customers. **The more intensive the rivalry, the less attractive is the industry.**==

**The six conditions in which rivalry turns cut-throat and industry profitability is low.** **(i) Industry Leader** — a strong industry leader can **discourage price wars by disciplining initiators**; because of its greater financial resources a leader can generally **outlast smaller rivals in a price war**, and knowing this, smaller rivals often avoid initiating such a contest. **(ii) Number of Competitors** — even when a leader exists, its ability to exert pricing discipline **diminishes with the increased number of rivals**, as communicating expectations to players becomes more difficult. **(iii) Fixed Costs** — rivals with **high fixed costs** feel strong motivation to utilise capacity and are therefore inclined to **cut prices when they have excess capacity**; price cutting causes profitability to fall for all firms, so profitability tends to be lower in industries characterised by high fixed costs. **(iv) Exit Barriers** — rivalry declines if some competitors leave, so **profitability tends to be higher in industries with few exit barriers**; assets of a firm considering exit may be **highly specialised and therefore of little value to any other firm**, so it can find no buyer and does not exit, and its continued presence exerts **downward pressure on the profitability of all competitors**. **(v) Product Differentiation** — firms can **insulate themselves from price wars** by differentiating, so profitability tends to be higher where differentiation is possible and **lower in industries involving undifferentiated commodities such as memory chips, natural resources, processed metals and railroads**. **(vi) Slow Growth** — industries whose growth is slowing face more intense rivalry, as rivals must **fight harder to grow or even to keep existing market share**.

**FORCE V — Threat of Substitutes.** ==**Substitute products are a latent source of competition** in an industry; in many cases they become a major constituent of competition.== Substitutes offering a **price advantage and/or performance improvement** to the consumer **can drastically alter the competitive character of an industry — and they can bring it about all of a sudden**. ICAI's example: **coir suffered at the hands of synthetic fibre.** ==Wherever **substantial investment in R&D** is taking place, threats from substitute products can be expected.== To predict profit pressure from this source, firms must **search for products that perform the same, or nearly the same, function** as their existing products — ICAI's example: **real estate, insurance, bonds and bank deposits are clear substitutes for common stocks**, because they represent alternate ways to invest funds.

**The forces together.** ==The five forces together determine industry attractiveness and profitability, because they influence the causes that underlie it== — elements such as the cost and investment needed to be a player in the industry are governed by these forces. **The collective strength of the five competitive forces determines the scope to earn attractive profits, and the strength of the forces may vary from industry to industry.**

The case gives nothing on buyers or substitutes — but ICAI's own answer still notes that domestic help is a substitute for a vacuum cleaner and that similar products let customers shift easily, which only intensifies rivalry.

**How to search:** to predict profit pressure from this source, firms must search for products that **perform the same, or nearly the same, function** as their existing products. Real estate, insurance, bonds and bank deposits are clear substitutes for common stocks, because they represent alternate ways to invest funds.
Substitutes usually **limit the prices and profits** in an industry, and so form one of the five pressures whose collective strength determines the scope for attractive profits.
keywords: perform the same, or nearly the same, function

official_questions.question: In light of the five forces as propagated by Michael Porter, explain the common barriers which may cause restrain for the keenness of new entrepreneurs. (5 Marks)
answer_points: In light of Michael Porter's Five Forces, new entrepreneurs often face significant barriers that restrain their keenness to enter an industry; these barriers increase the competitiveness of existing firms and discourage new entrants, impacting industry profitability.

**(i) Capital Requirements:** when a large amount of capital is required to enter an industry, firms lacking funds are effectively barred from the industry, thus enhancing the profitability of existing firms.

**(ii) Economies of Scale:** many industries are characterised by economic activities driven by economies of scale — the decline in the per-unit cost of production (or other activity) as volume grows.

**(iii) Product Differentiation:** the physical or perceptual differences, or enhancements, that make a product special or unique in the eyes of customers. **(iv) Switching Costs:** a new entrant must persuade existing customers of other companies to switch to its products; when switching costs are high, buyers are often reluctant to change.

**(v) Brand Identity:** the brand identity of products or services offered by existing firms is another entry barrier, particularly important for infrequently purchased products that carry a high unit cost to the buyer.

**(vi) Access to Distribution Channels:** the unavailability of distribution channels poses a significant barrier; despite the growing power of the internet many firms continue to rely on control of physical distribution channels. **(vii) Possibility of Aggressive Retaliation:** sometimes the mere threat of aggressive retaliation by incumbents can deter entry.
official_questions.examiner: No examiners' comments have been published for Paper 6.

MTP-M24-S2-SQ1c puts the same force to a case and is the cleanest short illustration of it: GreenThrift Inc., a sustainable clothing retailer enjoying a surge in popularity, is worried about **new sustainable fashion brands** using organic and recycled materials and ethical manufacturing. ICAI's answer: **"Competition from new sustainable fashion brands falls under the 'Threat of New Entrants' category of Porter's Five Forces Model for Competitive Analysis. These new entrants pose a threat to existing sustainable clothing retailers like GreenThrift Inc. by increasing competition and potentially eroding market share. The emergence of these brands, focusing on using organic and recycled materials along with ethical manufacturing practices, aligns with the values of environmentally conscious consumers, making them strong competitors in the sustainable fashion market."** Note what makes it a *new entrant* question rather than a rivalry question: the firms concerned are not yet in the market when the threat is assessed.

official_questions.question: As per one of the five forces of competition, Michael Porter stated that the more intensive is the rivalry, the less attractive is the industry. In view of this, explain the conditions in which rivalry among competitors tends to be cut throat and industry profitability is low. (5 Marks)
answer_points: **1. Industry Leader Presence:** while a strong industry leader can help maintain pricing discipline, the effectiveness diminishes as the number of competitors increases; many rivals can engage in aggressive pricing strategies, decreasing profitability.
**2. Number of Competitors:** a higher number of competitors increases rivalry, making it difficult for any single firm to control pricing, which leads to intensified price competition.

**3. High Fixed Costs:** industries with high fixed costs create pressure on firms to fully utilise capacity; when firms face excess capacity they resort to price cuts to maintain sales volume, which diminishes profitability across the industry.

**4. Exit Barriers:** high exit barriers prevent firms from leaving, keeping competition high; specialised assets or other constraints lead firms to remain in the market, maintaining competitive pressure and negatively impacting profitability for all players.

**5. Product Differentiation:** in industries lacking differentiation, firms primarily compete on price, leading to price wars and lower profitability; firms that can differentiate tend to achieve higher margins and reduce competitive pressure.

**6. Slow Industry Growth:** when growth slows, firms adopt aggressive tactics to protect or gain market share, intensifying rivalry and diminishing profitability as they compete for a limited customer base.
keywords: difficult for any single firm to control pricing

official_questions.question: Porter's five forces model hold that the state of competition in an industry is a composite of active competitive pressure in the market. Identify the areas of market in which competitive pressure operates. (5 Marks)
answer_points: Porter's Five Forces Model holds that the state of competition in an industry is a composite of competitive pressures operating in **five areas of the overall market**:
Competitive pressures associated with the **market manoeuvring and jockeying for buyer patronage** that goes on among rival sellers in the industry.
Competitive pressures associated with the **threat of new entrants** into the market.
Competitive pressures coming from the **attempts of companies in other industries to win buyers over to their own substitute products**.
Competitive pressures stemming from **supplier bargaining power and supplier-seller collaboration**.
Competitive pressures stemming from **buyer bargaining power and seller-buyer collaboration**.
official_questions.examiner: No examiners' comments have been published for Paper 6.

official_questions.question: According to Michael Porter, what are the five competitive forces that exist within an industry?
answer_points: **Threat of New Entrants:** new entrants bring added capacity and product variety, intensifying competition and impacting prices; the size of new entrants magnifies their competitive influence, placing constraints on prices and affecting existing players' profitability.

**Bargaining power of Buyers:** the ability of buyers to form groups or cartels influences their bargaining power; this force, particularly in industrial products, impacts pricing and often leads to demand for better services, influencing costs and investments for producers.

**Bargaining power of Suppliers:** suppliers with specialised offerings exert significant bargaining power, especially when limited in number; supplier bargaining power determines raw material costs, affecting industry attractiveness and profitability.

**Rivalry among Current Players:** existing players engage in competition, influencing strategic decisions across various levels; this rivalry is evident in pricing, advertising, cost pressures and product strategies.

**Threats from Substitutes:** substitute products can alter an industry's competitive dynamics, offering price advantages or performance improvements; substitutes limit prices and profits, and industries with substantial R&D investments are particularly susceptible.

**Closing line:** these forces collectively determine the industry's attractiveness and profitability by influencing factors such as the costs and investments required for industry participation; the strength of these forces varies across industries, ultimately shaping the potential for earning attractive profits.

official_questions.question: Easy Access is a marketing services company providing consultancy to a range of business clients. Easy Access and its rivals have managed to persuade the Government to require all marketing services companies to complete a time-consuming and bureaucratic registration process and to comply with an industry code of conduct. Do you think that by doing this Easy Access and its rivals has an advantage in some ways to fight off competitors? Explain.
answer_points: **Yes**, Easy Access and its rivals get an advantage from this move.

The new bureaucratic process is **making it more complicated for organisations to start up and enter the Easy Access market, increasing barriers to entry and thereby reducing the threat of new entrants**.

New entrants can reduce an industry's profitability because they **add new production capacity**, leading to an increase in supply of the product, sometimes even at a lower price, and can **substantially erode existing firms' market share position**.

New entrants are always a powerful source of competition: the new capacity and product range they bring in throws up new competitive pressure, and **the bigger the new entrant, the more severe the competitive effect**.
New entrants also **place a limit on prices and affect the profitability of existing players, which is known as Price War** — ICAI's own closing phrase in this answer.
keywords: reducing the threat of new entrants
also_asked_as: MTP-J25-S1-SQ3a sets the identical Easy Access case for 5 marks with the same published answer.

official_questions.question: Rajiv Arya owns an electrical appliance company specializing in the manufacture of domestic vacuum cleaners. The market is competitive, with four other manufacturers offering similar products and achieving comparable sales volumes. Additionally, these rival firms hold several patents related to the vacuum cleaner technology. The supplier base for raw materials is extensive, with multiple suppliers available. Identify and explain the significant forces from Porter's Five Forces framework that are relevant to Rajiv Arya's company.
answer_points: **Competitive rivalry** will be a significant force, as all the rivals are similar in size and manufacture similar products — it is difficult for any single manufacturer to dominate the market.
**Threat of new entrants is low:** a large number of patents will make it difficult for new entrants to break into the market.
**Bargaining power of suppliers is low:** as there are a large number of small suppliers, the power that suppliers can exert will be low.

**On the forces the case is silent about:** ICAI states that there is no information relating to substitutes and bargaining power of customers in the scenario — but reasons anyway that a domestic vacuum cleaner **directly competes with other options such as house maids**, and the availability of house maids at low cost can significantly disturb sales.
Further, as the products are similar, **customers can easily shift from one company to another, which will only enhance competitive rivalry**.
The lesson for presentation: name the forces the facts support, say explicitly where the facts are silent, and still reason about the silent force if a sensible substitute or buyer argument exists.
keywords: difficult for any single manufacturer to dominate
easily shift from one company to another

official_questions.question: Riya, the strategy manager of FreshSip Beverages Ltd., was studying the packaged fruit juice market in India before launching a new preservative-free juice brand. She observed that several established brands, low-priced local players, and substitute drinks like smoothies and flavored milk were competing intensely. Which aspect of external environment analysis is reflected in this situation?
answer_points: The situation reflects the **competitive environment (industry environment)** aspect of external environment analysis.

The competitive environment consists of factors **within the industry** that influence a firm's competitive position — existing competitors, new entrants, substitutes and pricing rivalry. Firms must evaluate industry structure and competitive forces before entering or expanding in a market.

In the given case Riya observed the presence of many established brands, low-cost local players and substitute beverages like smoothies and flavoured milk. This indicates **intense industry rivalry and a strong threat from substitutes**.
Such conditions affect profitability and market-entry decisions.
Therefore FreshSip must assess competitive forces and develop appropriate strategies such as **differentiation or cost competitiveness** to succeed.

official_questions.question: Buyers can exert considerable pressure on business. Do you agree? Discuss. (5 Marks)
answer_points: **Yes.** Buyers of an industry's products or services can sometimes exert considerable pressure on existing firms to secure **lower prices or better services**. This is evident in situations where buyers enjoy a superior position to the seller of the product.
The leverage is particularly evident when **(i)** buyers have **full knowledge of the sources of products and their substitutes**;
**(ii)** they **spend a lot of money on the industry's products, i.e. they are big buyers**;

**(iii)** the industry's product is **not perceived as critical to the buyer's needs** and buyers are **more concentrated than the firms supplying** the product, so they can easily switch to the substitutes available.

Buyer power is heavier where buyers can form **groups or cartels** — mostly seen in industrial products — and it influences not only prices but also the producer's **costs and investments**, because powerful buyers bargain for better services.

mcqs.question: EcoRide Motors, an Indian electric scooter company, faces rising competition from new EV start-ups offering affordable models. Battery suppliers have raised costs due to global shortages, while customers now compare multiple brands online before purchase. Traditional petrol scooter manufacturers are also entering the EV segment. EcoRide struggles to maintain profitability despite growing market demand. Which force poses the greatest threat to EcoRide's profitability?
mcqs.explanation: New start-ups, petrol manufacturers entering the segment and price-comparing customers all converge on intensifying rivalry, and 'the more intensive the rivalry, the less attractive is the industry' (SM §2.5.1). ICAI key: (c).

why_wrong.A: Petrol scooters are rivals in the same industry segment, not substitutes from another industry.
why_wrong.B: Supplier cost pressure is present but is one of four pressures described, not the greatest.
why_wrong.D: Buyers compare brands but are not concentrated big buyers.

mcqs.trap: Four forces are deliberately seeded in the stem; the question asks which is greatest.

mcqs.question: When EcoRide attempted to enter the budget scooter market but failed due to intense competition and thin margins, which of Porter's Five Forces best explains the challenge, and how did it affect profitability?
mcqs.explanation: Intense competition with thin margins is the signature of cut-throat rivalry — undifferentiated products and price competition drive profitability down for all (SM §2.5.1). ICAI key: (c).

why_wrong.A: No alternative product from another industry is named.
why_wrong.B: No input supplier is named here.
why_wrong.D: No buyer concentration is named.

mcqs.trap: 'Failed to enter' tempts 'threat of new entrants'; but EcoRide was itself the entrant, and the force it ran into was existing rivalry.

mcqs.question: In the smartphone industry, if a few large component manufacturers control the supply of specialised OLED screens and there are no viable alternative suppliers, the smartphone brands face high pressure from:
mcqs.explanation: Suppliers command bargaining power when their products are crucial to the buyer and substitutes are not available, and when they are limited in number and more concentrated than their buyers (SM §2.5.1). ICAI key: (c).

why_wrong.A: The smartphone brands are the buyers here, not the pressurising party.
why_wrong.B: 'No viable alternative suppliers' is the absence of substitute *inputs*, which is a condition of supplier power, not the substitutes force.
why_wrong.D: No rival behaviour is described.

mcqs.trap: The words 'no viable alternative' pull towards 'substitutes'; in Porter's model, the absence of substitute inputs is what *gives* suppliers their power.

mcqs.question: Which key industry force, as per Porter's Five Forces, is reflected in EcoForge's challenges from cheaper alternatives and intense competition?
mcqs.explanation: 'Cheaper alternatives' are substitute products offering a price advantage, which the study material says can drastically alter the competitive character of an industry. ICAI key: (D).

why_wrong.A: No new firm entering is described.
why_wrong.B: No input supplier is described.
why_wrong.C: No buyer concentration is described.

mcqs.trap: 'Intense competition' tempts rivalry, but the distinctive fact is the cheaper alternative.

mcqs.question: In the Indian smartphone market, Chinese brands completely captured the budget segment. Which of Porter's Five Forces is intensified by the presence of numerous players offering functionally similar, low-priced products?
mcqs.explanation: Numerous players with undifferentiated products competing on price is precisely the study material's condition for cut-throat rivalry — number of competitors plus lack of product differentiation. ICAI key: (A).

why_wrong.B: No input supplier is described.
why_wrong.C: The brands have already captured the segment; they are incumbents now.
why_wrong.D: Buyers are fragmented consumers.

mcqs.trap: 'Captured the segment' suggests new entrants; the force intensified by *numerous* similar players is rivalry.

mcqs.question: How did Zing protect its market share from potential competitors?
mcqs.explanation: Brand identity and switching costs are two of the seven barriers to entry: buyers incur substantial financial and psychological costs in switching, and brand identity requires substantial resources committed over a long period (SM §2.5.1). ICAI key: (b).

why_wrong.A: Price cutting is a rivalry tactic that lowers everyone's profitability.
why_wrong.C: Advertising is the incumbents' *retaliation* response, not what protected the share here.
why_wrong.D: International expansion is a growth choice, not an entry barrier.

mcqs.trap: All four are real competitive actions; only two of the seven published barriers appear in one option.

mcqs.question: Kanika, known as "Desi Taylor Swift", launched the lipstick brand Kolor among intense global and domestic competition. Despite a lack of groundwork, her substantial 45 million social media following gained significant attention. Which aspect of Michael Porter's force multiplier is working in favour of Kolor?
mcqs.explanation: Kolor *is* the new entrant, and an established following has lowered the barriers that would normally keep it out — brand identity and access to distribution among them. The force working in its favour is therefore the threat of new entrants, which is high where entry barriers are low. ICAI key: (b).

why_wrong.A: Social media influence is not one of Porter's five forces; it is the *reason* the entry barrier is low.
why_wrong.C: No supplier concentration or switching issue is described.
why_wrong.D: No buyer concentration or price pressure is described.

mcqs.trap: Option A restates the stem's own fact and is not a force at all — the classic distractor in a five-forces MCQ. Name the force, not the circumstance.

mcqs.question: Which of the following is **not** one of the seven barriers to entry listed in the study material?
mcqs.explanation: SM §2.5.1 lists capital requirements, economies of scale, product differentiation, switching costs, brand identity, access to distribution channels and possibility of aggressive retaliation. Government ownership is not among them.

why_wrong.A: Listed, seventh.
why_wrong.B: Listed, sixth.
why_wrong.D: Listed, fourth.

mcqs.trap: Government ownership is a real-world barrier but is not in the published list; the political-legal environment covers it instead.

mcqs.question: As per the study material, profitability tends to be **higher** in industries:
mcqs.explanation: SM §2.5.1: 'Rivalry among competitors declines if some competitors leave an industry. Profitability therefore tends to be higher in industries with few exit barriers.'

why_wrong.A: High fixed costs push firms to cut prices when they have excess capacity, lowering profitability.
why_wrong.C: Slowing growth intensifies rivalry and reduces profitability.
why_wrong.D: Undifferentiated commodities — memory chips, natural resources, processed metals, railroads — show lower profitability.

mcqs.trap: The intuitive answer is that high exit barriers protect incumbents; the study material says the opposite, because trapped rivals keep competing.

mcqs.question: According to the study material, Michael Porter believes the basic unit of analysis for understanding competition is:

options.A: The individual firm and its resources
options.C: A group of competitors producing goods or services that compete directly with each other

mcqs.explanation: SM §2.5.1: Porter believes the basic unit of analysis is a group of competitors producing goods or services that compete directly with each other — it is the industry where competitive advantage is ultimately won or lost.

why_wrong.A: The resource view of the firm is the Chapter 3 perspective.
why_wrong.B: The national economy is the macro environment.
why_wrong.D: Customer segments belong to customer analysis (§2.6.2).

mcqs.trap: Porter is also associated with the value chain, which is firm-level; his *competition* unit of analysis is the industry.

mcqs.question: In the three-step use of the Five Forces model, the strategist's **second** step is to:

options.A: Identify the specific competitive pressures associated with each of the five forces
options.B: Determine whether the collective strength of the forces is conducive to earning attractive profits
options.C: Draw circles proportional to each group's share of industry sales
options.D: Evaluate how strong the pressures comprising each of the five forces are — fierce, strong, moderate to normal, or weak

mcqs.explanation: SM §2.5.1: Step 1 identify the pressures; Step 2 evaluate how strong each is (fierce, strong, moderate to normal, weak); Step 3 determine whether collective strength is conducive to attractive profits.

why_wrong.A: That is Step 1.
why_wrong.B: That is Step 3.
why_wrong.C: That is Step 4 of strategic group mapping (§2.7.1), a different tool.

mcqs.trap: Option C belongs to a different four-step procedure in the same chapter.

recap: Five forces: new entrants, buyer power, supplier power, rivalry, substitutes; their interrelationship gives each industry its own competitive environment.
Five areas of pressure (ICAI's own wording): jockeying among rival sellers, threat of entry, other industries' substitutes, supplier power and collaboration, buyer power and collaboration.
Three steps: identify pressures → rate each fierce/strong/moderate/weak → judge collective strength.
Seven barriers: capital, economies of scale, differentiation, switching costs, brand identity, distribution channels, aggressive retaliation.
Buyer power when: full knowledge of sources and substitutes · big buyers · product not critical and buyers more concentrated.
Supplier power when: products crucial and no substitutes · high switching costs · more concentrated than buyers.
Cut-throat rivalry: leader, number of competitors, high fixed costs, exit barriers, no differentiation, slow growth.
Substitutes are latent, can change an industry all of a sudden, and come from products performing the same or nearly the same function.

concepts.title: 2.5.2 Attractiveness of Industry
concepts.evidence: PYQ 0 · RTP 0 · MTP 0 (appears only as the second half of five-forces answers)
understand: ==**The industry analysis culminates into identification of various issues and draws conclusions about the relative attractiveness or unattractiveness of the industry, both near-term and long-term.**== Strategists assess the industry outlook carefully, deciding whether industry and competitive conditions present an **attractive business opportunity** or whether growth and profit prospects are **gloomy**. This matters because companies invest capital — either the promoters' or from the public — and **should be inherently careful in choosing an industry**.
**The nine factors on which management may base such conclusions:**
**(i)** The industry's **growth potential** — is it futuristically viable?
**(ii)** Whether **competition currently permits adequate profitability**, and whether competitive forces will become **stronger or weaker**.
**(iii)** Whether industry profitability will be **favourably or unfavourably affected by the prevailing driving forces**.

**(iv)** The **competitive position of the organisation** in the industry and whether that position is likely to grow stronger or weaker. ICAI's parenthesis is important: ==being a **well-entrenched leader or strongly positioned contender in an otherwise lacklustre industry can still produce good profitability**; however, having to **fight an uphill battle against much stronger rivals can make an otherwise attractive industry unattractive**.==
**(v)** The **potential to capitalise on the vulnerabilities of weaker rivals** — perhaps converting an unattractive industry situation into a potentially rewarding company opportunity.
**(vi)** Whether the company is **able to defend against or counteract the factors** that make the industry unattractive.
**(vii)** The **degrees of risk and uncertainty** in the industry's future.
**(viii)** The **severity of problems confronting the industry as a whole**.
**(ix)** Whether **continued participation in this industry adds importantly to the firm's ability to be successful in other industries** in which it may have business interests.

**The general proposition and its qualification.** As a general proposition, ==if an industry's overall profit prospects are **above average**, the industry can be considered **attractive**; if below average, it is **unattractive**. However, **it is a mistake to think of industries as being attractive or unattractive to all firms in the industry and all potential entrants** — **attractiveness is relative, not absolute.** Industry environments unattractive to weak competitors may be attractive to strong competitors.==

**What follows from the verdict.** An assessment that the industry is **fundamentally attractive** typically suggests that current participants employ strategies calculated to **strengthen their long-term competitive positions**, expanding sales efforts and investing in additional facilities and equipment as needed.

If the industry and competitive situation is judged **relatively unattractive**, more successful participants may choose to **invest cautiously**, look for ways to **protect their long-term competitiveness and profitability**, and perhaps **acquire smaller firms if the price is right**; over the longer term, strong companies may consider **diversification into more attractive businesses**.

**Weak companies in unattractive industries** may consider **merging with a rival to bolster market share and profitability** or, alternatively, **begin looking outside the industry for attractive diversification opportunities**.
concepts.example: Two firms look at the same slow-growing, price-competitive packaging industry. The entrenched leader with the lowest costs reads it as attractive and funds a new plant. A sub-scale follower reads the same industry as unattractive and merges with a rival to bolster share. Both readings are correct — that is what 'attractiveness is relative, not absolute' means.

inherent careful in choosing an industry
lacklustre industry can still produce good profitability
uphill battle against much stronger rivals
acquire smaller firms if the price is right
merging with a rival to bolster market share

memory.trick: Three strategic postures follow the verdict — **Strong firm + attractive industry** = expand and invest; **strong firm + unattractive industry** = invest cautiously, protect, buy cheap, then diversify; **weak firm + unattractive industry** = merge or leave.

Invest cautiously; protect competitiveness; acquire smaller firms if the price is right; later diversify

Giving only the growth-potential factor. The published list has nine factors, and the firm's own competitive position is one of them.

Ignoring the near-term/long-term split. The conclusion must be drawn 'both near-term and long-term'.

expected_questions.question: "Attractiveness is relative, not absolute." Explain how a strategist concludes on the attractiveness of an industry, and what strategies follow from the conclusion.
answer_points: Industry analysis culminates in conclusions about the relative attractiveness or unattractiveness of the industry, **both near-term and long-term**; companies invest the promoters' or the public's capital and should be careful in choosing an industry.

**The factors considered:** growth potential and futuristic viability; whether competition currently permits adequate profitability and whether the forces will strengthen or weaken; whether prevailing driving forces will affect profitability favourably or unfavourably; the firm's own competitive position and whether it will grow stronger or weaker; the potential to capitalise on the vulnerabilities of weaker rivals; the ability to defend against or counteract the unattractive factors; the degrees of risk and uncertainty; the severity of problems confronting the industry as a whole; and whether continued participation adds importantly to the firm's success in other industries.
**The general proposition:** above-average overall profit prospects make an industry attractive; below-average prospects make it unattractive.

**The qualification:** it is a mistake to think of industries as attractive or unattractive to all firms and all potential entrants — attractiveness is relative, not absolute. Environments unattractive to weak competitors may be attractive to strong ones; a well-entrenched leader in a lacklustre industry can still earn good profits, while an uphill battle against much stronger rivals can make an otherwise attractive industry unattractive.

**Strategies that follow:** if attractive, strengthen long-term competitive positions, expand sales efforts and invest in facilities. If unattractive, successful participants invest cautiously, protect long-term competitiveness and profitability, perhaps acquire smaller firms if the price is right, and over the longer term consider diversification. Weak companies in unattractive industries may merge with a rival to bolster market share and profitability, or look outside the industry for diversification opportunities.

options.A: Attractiveness is relative, not absolute — an environment unattractive to weak competitors may be attractive to strong ones
options.B: An industry with below-average profit prospects is unattractive to every firm in it
options.C: Attractiveness is judged only in the long term, since near-term conditions fluctuate
options.D: A well-entrenched leader in a lacklustre industry cannot earn good profitability

mcqs.explanation: SM §2.5.2: 'Attractiveness is relative, not absolute. Industry environments unattractive to weak competitors may be attractive to strong competitors.'

why_wrong.B: The study material calls it a mistake to think of industries as attractive or unattractive to all firms and all potential entrants.
why_wrong.C: Conclusions are drawn both near-term and long-term.

mcqs.question: A weak company in an industry judged relatively unattractive is, as per the study material, likely to:

options.A: Expand sales efforts and invest in additional facilities and equipment
options.B: Acquire several larger rivals to gain scale
options.C: Consider merging with a rival to bolster market share and profitability, or look outside the industry for diversification opportunities

why_wrong.B: The study material refers to acquiring **smaller** firms if the price is right, and that option belongs to strong participants.

recap: Industry analysis culminates in a near-term and long-term attractiveness verdict.
Nine factors, including the firm's own competitive position and the ability to exploit weaker rivals.
Above-average prospects = attractive; below-average = unattractive — but attractiveness is relative, not absolute.
Attractive → strengthen position, expand, invest. Unattractive and strong → invest cautiously, protect, buy small firms cheap, later diversify. Unattractive and weak → merge or look outside.

concepts.title: 2.5.3 Experience Curve
understand: ==**The experience curve is akin to a learning curve, which explains the efficiency increase gained by workers through repetitive productive work.** The experience curve is based on the commonly observed phenomenon that **unit costs decline as a firm accumulates experience in terms of a cumulative volume of production**. It is based on the concept, **"we learn as we grow"**.==
==**The implication** is that **larger firms in an industry would tend to have lower unit costs as compared to those for smaller companies, thereby gaining a competitive cost advantage.**==

**The experience curve results from a variety of factors:** **learning effects, economies of scale, product redesign and technological improvements in production.** Note that economies of scale is only *one* of the four causes — the experience curve is not a synonym for scale economies.

**The three features of the experience curve:** **(i)** as business organisations grow, **they gain experience**; **(ii)** experience may provide an **advantage over the competition** — ==**experience is a key barrier to entry**==; **(iii)** **large and successful organisations possess a stronger "experience effect"**.

concepts.evidence: PYQ 0 · RTP 0 · MTP 0 — a heading added in the 2026 syllabus edition and not yet examined
understand: **The concept of value creation** was introduced primarily for providing products and services to customers **with more worth**. ==**Value is measured by a product's features, quality, availability, durability, performance and by its services, for which customers are willing to pay.**== The concept later took more space in business, and organisations started discussing **value creation for stakeholders**.

==**Value creation is an activity or performance by the firm to create value that increases the worth of goods, services, business processes or even the whole business system.**== Many businesses now focus on value creation both for **customers purchasing its products and services** and for **stakeholders in the business who want to see their investment appreciate in value**. Ultimately the concept gives a business a **competitive advantage in the industry** and helps it earn **above average profits/returns**.

**The profitable pricing band.** The chapter's figure sets out the arithmetic of value creation on a single vertical scale: at the bottom is the **firm's cost of value creation**; above it is the **price**; above that, the **value to customer**. The gap between price and cost is the **firm's margin**; the gap between value to customer and price is the **customer's surplus**; and the whole band between cost and value to customer is the **profitable pricing band**. ==**It is basically the value the consumer wants to pay, over and above the price that the business wants to charge from the consumer. This excess amount is called value creation, wherein the consumers value the product or service more than it actually costs them.**==

**Competitive advantage leads to superior profitability.** ==At the most basic level, how profitable a company becomes depends on **three factors**: **(1) the value customers place on the company's products; (2) the price that a company charges for its products; and (3) the costs of creating those products.**==

**Utility versus price.** The value customers place on a product reflects the **utility** they get from it — **the happiness or satisfaction gained from consuming or owning the product**. ==**Utility must be distinguished from price. Utility is something that customers get from a product**; it is a function of the attributes of the product, such as its **performance, design, quality, and point-of-sale and after-sale service**.==

**Porter's two routes.** Companies ultimately aim to achieve **sustainable competitive advantage**, which enables them to succeed in the long run. ==Michael Porter argues that a company can generate competitive advantage in **two different ways, either through differentiation or cost advantage**.== According to Porter, **differentiation means the capability to provide customers superior and special value in the form of a product's special features and quality, or in the form of after-sales customer service**. As a result of differentiation a company **can demand a higher price** for its products or services, and it will earn higher profits from differentiation **in case the expenses stay comparable to the costs of competitors**.

**Why the value chain follows.** Differentiation and cost advantage affect a company's ability to achieve competitive advantage, but **many different organisational functions influence whether a company can achieve either**. ==Michael Porter used the concept of the **value chain** to explore more closely the different functions of organisations and the mutual interactions among them: **value chain analysis provides an excellent tool to examine the origin of competitive advantage**, dividing the organisation into **two strategically important groups of activities — primary activities and supporting activities** — which help comprehend the **potential sources for differentiation** and understand an **organisation's cost behaviour**.==
concepts.example: A premium water purifier costs the maker ₹6,000, sells at ₹11,000, and a buyer who values the health benefit and the five-year service plan would have paid ₹14,000. The firm's margin is ₹5,000, the customer's surplus is ₹3,000, and the profitable pricing band runs from ₹6,000 to ₹14,000. The ₹3,000 the customer keeps is the value created — and it is what makes the purchase feel worth more than it cost.

concepts.title: 2.6–2.6.1 Market and Customer; Customer
concepts.evidence: PYQ 0 · RTP 0 · MTP 0 — headings added in the 2026 syllabus edition
understand: ==**A market is a place for interested parties, buyers and sellers, where items and services can be exchanged for a price.**== The market might be **physical**, such as a departmental store where people engage in person, or **virtual**, such as an online market where buyers and sellers do not meet in person but use tools of technology to strike a deal.

The term market applies to a **wide range of contexts**: the **stock exchange**, where securities are traded; a **group of individuals trying to buy a specific commodity or service in a specific place**, such as a grain or vegetable market where farmers come to sell their produce; and a **business or industry**, such as the global oil market.

**Market versus marketing.** ==While the market is a **place**, business strategists work on **marketing** to improve the chances of success.== The term marketing encompasses a wide range of operations, including **research, designing, pricing, promotion, transportation and distribution**.

==**The four Ps of marketing — product, place, pricing and promotion.**== Market activities are often categorised and explained in terms of these four, which **help marketers identify customer needs so they may meet their demands and deliver satisfaction**. ==**Delivering the best customer experience and establishing, maintaining and growing relationships with customers are the main goals of marketing.**==
**The four orientations of product marketing.** The orientation of product marketing has evolved and acquired different dimensions centred around **product, production, sales and customers**:
**(i) Product orientation** — businesses think that **buyers will choose those products that have the best quality, performance, design, or features**.
**(ii) Production orientation** — businesses believe that **customers choose low price products**.
**(iii) Sales orientation** — businesses believe that **if they spend enough money on advertisement, sales and promotion, customers can be persuaded to make a purchase**.

**(iv) Customer or market orientation** — ==strategists **prioritise efforts on their customers**. In order to create better value propositions, businesses **gather, disseminate and use customer and competitive information**. A customer-centric business is one that **continuously learns from its customers' needs and market dynamics**. In the present times, the success of many businesses lies in customer-centric approaches.==

**Customer (§2.6.1).** ==**A customer is a person or business that buys products or services from another organisation.** Customers are important because **they provide revenue and organisations cannot exist without them**.== All businesses vie for customers, either by **aggressively marketing their products or by lowering their pricing to boost their customer bases**.

**Customer versus consumer — the thin distinction.** The terms are practically synonymous and are frequently used interchangeably, but there is a thin distinction. ==**Individuals or businesses that consume or utilise products and services are referred to as consumers. Customers are the purchasers of products and services in the economy, and they might exist as consumers or only as customers.**== ICAI's illustration: **in homes, groceries are often bought by a parent and consumed by all the members of the family.**

**Why firms research customer characteristics.** Businesses routinely research the characteristics of their consumers **in order to fine-tune their marketing strategies and adjust their inventory to attract the most customers**. ==Customers are frequently **categorised based on demographics such as age, race, gender, ethnicity, economic level and geographic region**, which may all assist businesses in **developing a profile of a perfect customer**.==
concepts.example: A cloud-services firm sells an enterprise subscription to a company's procurement head — the **customer** — while the employees who actually use the software are the **consumers**. **What customer analysis includes — five activities:** **(i)** the **administration of customer surveys**; **(ii)** the **study of consumer data**; **(iii)** the **evaluation of market positioning strategies**; **(iv)** the **development of customer profiles**; and **(v)** the **selection of the best market segmentation techniques**.
==Using the facts generated by customer analysis, an **effective profiling of customers** may be established. **Customer profiles can reveal demographic information about customers.**==

**Who can help gather the information.** ==A number of parties can assist: **buyers, sellers, distributors, salespeople, managers, wholesalers, retailers, suppliers and creditors.**== Note how wide that list is — it reaches beyond the firm's own staff into the whole channel and even its creditors.

==**Successful businesses constantly monitor the behaviour of existing and prospective customers.**== That sentence is the bridge into §2.6.3: customer analysis identifies *who* the customers are and *what* they want; customer behaviour explains *how* they buy.

Read the two passages together: segments come from the segmentation techniques, motivations from the surveys and consumer data, and unmet needs from the evaluation of needs, desires and wants.

Those are the five published activities of customer analysis, in order.

concepts.title: 2.6.3 Customer Behaviour
understand: ==**Customer behaviour moves beyond the identification of customers to explain how they purchase products.** It examines elements like **shopping frequency, product preferences, and the perception of your marketing, sales, and service offerings.**== Understanding these details allows businesses to **communicate with customers in an effective manner**.

==Understanding the behaviours of customers enables businesses to **establish effective marketing and advertising campaigns, provide products and services that meet their needs, and retain customers for repeat sales**.==

**The conceptual domains.** The study material says consumer behaviour may be influenced by a number of things, and that these elements **can be categorised into the following three conceptual domains** — then prints **four** headings: External Influences, Internal Influences, Decision Making and Post-decision Processes. ==**This is an inconsistency in ICAI's own text**: the sentence says three, the list has four. ICAI's published answers resolve it both ways — MTP Jan 2025 Series 1 says 'the following conceptual domains' and gives four, while MTP Jan 2026 Series 2 says consumer behaviour 'is influenced by **four** major conceptual domains' and gives four. **Write four, and name them all**; a question that asks for 'the three conceptual domains' is still answered safely with the four headings.==

**(1) External Influences.** ==External influences, **like advertisement, peer recommendations or social norms**, have a **direct impact on the psychological and internal processes** that influence various consumer decisions.== The focus of external effects is on the numerous elements that have an impact on customers **as they choose which needs to satisfy and which products to use** to do so. ==These aspects are divided into **two groups — the company's marketing efforts and the numerous environmental elements.**==

**(2) Internal Influences.** ==**Internal processes are psychological factors internal to the customer and affect consumer decision making.**== Consumer behaviour is influenced by a **combination of internal and external influences, including motivation and attitudes**.

**The process figure.** The chapter's diagram shows **External Factors** (market stimuli, environmental factors) and **Internal Factors** both feeding **Decision Making**, which leads to **Purchase and Post Purchase Actions**.

**(3) Decision Making.** ==**A rational consumer, as decision maker, would seek information about potential decisions and carefully integrate this with the existing knowledge about the product. After weighing the advantages and disadvantages of each option, they would make a decision.**== The **four stages** of the decision-making process are: **(i) Problem recognition** — identify an existing need or desire that is unfulfilled; **(ii) Search for desirable alternatives and list them**; **(iii) Seeking information on available alternatives and weighing their pros and cons**; **(iv) Make a final choice**.

==This behaviour of making decisions happens very frequently. **However, it mostly applies when the purchase is one that is significant to the customer**, such as when the product could have a significant influence on their **health or self-image**. The process is **extremely valid when purchasing a car, television or a refrigerator, in contrast to the purchase of ice creams or soft drinks.**==

**(4) Post-decision Processes.** ==After making a decision and purchasing a product, the final phase is **evaluating the outcome**. The consumer's reaction may vary depending upon the satisfaction: **a happy customer may make a repeat purchase and recommend it to others, while a customer with dissonance will neither purchase the product again nor recommend it to others.**==
concepts.example: A luxury skincare brand's sales jump after celebrity endorsements. External influences (the endorsement and social-media promotion) act on internal influences (aspirational self-image, altered perception of quality), which speed up the four-stage decision process by reducing perceived risk; whether the spike lasts depends on the post-decision phase — satisfied buyers repeat and recommend, dissonant ones do neither. That is ICAI's own answer structure for exactly this case.

official_questions.question: You are a strategic manager for a tech company launching a new smartphone model. The company wants to target tech-savvy consumers who value innovation and cutting-edge technology. Using the concept of customer behavior, develop a marketing strategy to promote the new smartphone. (5 Marks)
answer_points: To target tech-savvy consumers the company can develop a marketing strategy based on customer behaviour, whose influences fall into the following conceptual domains.

**External Influences:** utilise online platforms and tech forums to generate buzz around the new smartphone; partner with tech influencers and bloggers to review the product and create awareness among tech-savvy consumers.
**Internal Influences:** appeal to the desire for innovation and advanced features; highlight the unique selling points of the smartphone — its cutting-edge technology, performance and design.

**Decision Making:** recognise that tech-savvy consumers are early adopters who value functionality and performance; provide detailed specifications and comparisons with other smartphones to help them make an informed decision.

**Post-decision Processes:** offer excellent customer service and support to address any technical issues or concerns; encourage customers to provide feedback and reviews to build credibility and trust among tech-savvy consumers.
By understanding the behaviour of tech-savvy consumers and aligning the marketing strategy with their preferences, the company can effectively promote the new smartphone and attract this demographic.

official_questions.question: A luxury skincare brand saw a sudden spike in sales after celebrity endorsements and social media promotions. What factors could be influencing this change in consumer buying behavior, and why is understanding such behavior critical to business success? (5 Marks)
answer_points: The surge is explained through the framework of **Consumer Behaviour**, which goes beyond identifying customers and focuses on how they purchase products, their preferences, perceptions and shopping patterns. ICAI states here that consumer behaviour is influenced by **four major conceptual domains**.

**1. External Influences:** advertisements, celebrity endorsements, peer recommendations and social norms. Here the endorsements and social-media promotions acted as strong **marketing stimuli**, directly shaping how consumers perceived the brand and influencing their decision to purchase.

**2. Internal Influences:** psychological processes within the consumer — motivation, attitudes and perception. The promotions may have altered the consumer's perception of the product's quality and created motivation linked to **beauty, self-image or aspirational lifestyles**.

**3. Decision-Making Process:** problem recognition → search for alternatives → information seeking and evaluation → final choice. The endorsements helped consumers recognise the product as a desirable solution, provided information and **reduced perceived risk**, leading to quicker and more confident decision-making.

**4. Post-Decision Processes:** satisfied customers will repeat their purchase and recommend the brand, sustaining the increased sales; dissatisfied customers may experience **dissonance** and not return.

**Why it is critical:** understanding customer behaviour — its external and internal influences, decision-making stages and post-purchase reactions — enables businesses to communicate effectively, design relevant marketing campaigns, deliver products that meet consumer needs and retain customers for repeat sales.

concepts.title: 2.7 Competitive Strategy
concepts.evidence: PYQ 0 · RTP 0 · MTP 1 (as a secondary code)
understand: ==**Competition is a fundamental attribute of economic systems and business**, and it is frequently connected with small and large organisations alike. **Businesses compete with each other for the same set of resources and customers.**== Within an industry, competition is frequently encouraged with the **wider goal of attaining and achieving higher quality services or superior goods** that the firm may manufacture or develop.

==**The competitive strategy of a business is concerned with how to compete in the business areas in which the organization operates.** In other words, **competitive strategy defines how a firm expects to create and sustain a competitive advantage over competitors.** Having a competitive advantage over competitors means **being more profitable in the long run**.==

==**The competitive strategy of a firm within a certain business field is analysed using two criteria: the creation of competitive advantage and the protection of competitive advantage.**== Those two criteria are the heart of this heading — create it, then protect it.

**Why the analysis matters.** An important component of industry and competitive analysis involves **delving into the industry's competitive process to discover what the main sources of competitive pressure are and how strong each competitive force is**. ==This analytical step is **essential because managers cannot devise a successful strategy without in-depth understanding of the industry's competitive character**.== Even though competitive pressures in various industries are never precisely the same, **the competitive process works similarly enough to use a common analytical framework** in gauging the nature and intensity of competitive forces.

==**Porter's five forces model is useful in understanding the competition.** It is a powerful tool for **systematically diagnosing the main competitive pressures in a market and assessing how strong and important each one is**. Not only is it the widely used technique of competition analysis, but it is also **relatively easy to understand and apply**.==

Read this heading as the bridge of the chapter's last section: §2.7 states *what* competitive strategy is and *which* framework serves it; §2.7.1 supplies the tool for mapping rivals (the competitive landscape); §2.7.2 supplies the test of what matters most in the industry (key success factors).
concepts.example: A regional dairy decides it will compete on cold-chain reliability rather than price. Creating that advantage means investing in chillers and routing software; protecting it means long-term farmer contracts and exclusive retail freezers. The 'how to compete' choice plus those two criteria — creation and protection — are its competitive strategy.

concepts.title: 2.7.1 Competitive Landscape (and Strategic Group Mapping)
understand: ==**Competitive landscape is a business analysis which identifies competitors, either direct or indirect.**== It is about **identifying and understanding the competitors** and at the same time it **permits the comprehension of their vision, mission, core values, niche market, strengths and weaknesses**. ==Understanding the competitive landscape **requires an application of "competitive intelligence"**.==

==An **in-depth investigation and analysis of a firm's competition** allows it to **assess the competitors' strengths and weaknesses in the marketplace** and helps it to **choose and implement effective strategies that will improve its competitive advantage**. Thus, **understanding the competitive landscape is important to build upon a competitive advantage.**==
**The five steps to understand the competitive landscape** — the single most-examined list in SM Chapter 2, with the questions each step answers:

**(i) Identify the competitor.** The first step is to identify the competitors in the firm's industry and **have actual data about their respective market share**. ==*This answers: Who are the competitors and how big are they?*==

**(ii) Understand the competitors.** Once identified, the strategist can use **market research reports, the internet, newspapers, social media, industry reports and various other sources** to understand the products and services offered by them **in different markets**. ==*This answers: What are their products and services?*==

**(iii) Determine the strengths of the competitors.** What are their strengths? What do they do well? Do they offer great products? Why are consumers liking their product or service? Do they utilise marketing in a way that comparatively reaches out to more consumers? Why do customers give them their business? ==*This answers: What are their financial positions? What gives them cost and price advantage? What are they likely to do next? How strong is their distribution network? What are their human resource strengths?*==

**(iv) Determine the weaknesses of the competitors.** Identify the areas where the competitor is lacking or weak. Weaknesses (and strengths) can be identified by **going through consumer reports and reviews appearing in various media**; **financial strength and weakness can always be learnt from annual reports**. ==*This answers: Where are they lacking?*==

**(v) Put all of the information together.** The strategist should put together all information about competitors and **draw inference about what they are not offering and what the firm can do to fill in the gaps**; the strategist can also know the areas which need to be strengthened by the firm. ==*This answers: What will the business do with this information? What improvements does the firm need to make? How can the firm exploit the weaknesses of competitors?*==

**Strategic group mapping — the companion tool.** ICAI treats this as the tool to use whenever a case asks for the **market positions of rival companies grouped into like positions**. ==**A strategic group consists of those rival firms which have similar competitive approaches and positions in the market.**==

**The four-step procedure for constructing a strategic group map:** ==**(1) Identify the competitive characteristics that differentiate firms in the industry** — the typical variables being **price/quality range (high, medium, low); geographic coverage (local, regional, national, global); degree of vertical integration (none, partial, full); product-line breadth (wide, narrow); use of distribution channels (one, some, all); and degree of service offered (no-frills, limited, full)**. **(2) Plot the firms on a two-variable map** using pairs of these differentiating characteristics. **(3) Assign firms that fall in about the same strategy space to the same strategic group.** **(4) Draw circles around each strategic group, making the circles proportional to the size of the group's respective share of total industry sales revenues.**==

**The insights a map yields** (from ICAI's May 2026 MTP answer): it helps understand competitive positioning, **identifies direct competitors within the same strategic group**, reveals **market gaps or opportunities** such as underserved segments, highlights **mobility barriers between groups** — the difficulty of moving from the low-end to the premium segment — and assists in analysing the **intensity of competition within and across groups**.

**ICAI's labelling tension, recorded rather than smoothed over.** ICAI's RTPs print their own chapter headings, and in some RTPs the strategic-group-mapping question is printed under **Chapter 3**, although the register places Competitive Landscape at S02.23 in Chapter 2. This book follows the register and keeps all strategic-group-mapping material here, where the five steps and the four-step procedure sit together. The practical consequence for a candidate is nil — the answer is the same either way — but it explains why the same question can be found under two chapter labels in ICAI's own material.

The map shows that no one occupies 'premium, narrow range, health-positioned' — the gap the new line will fill. That is strategic group mapping answering a competitive-landscape question.

expected_questions.question: What is a strategic group? Explain the procedure for constructing a strategic group map, and state the insights such a map can yield.
answer_points: A **strategic group** consists of those rival firms which have **similar competitive approaches and positions in the market**. Strategic group mapping is the tool used to identify the market positions of rival companies by grouping them into like positions.

**Step 1:** identify the competitive characteristics that differentiate firms in the industry — typical variables are price/quality range (high, medium, low); geographic coverage (local, regional, national, global); degree of vertical integration (none, partial, full); product-line breadth (wide, narrow); use of distribution channels (one, some, all); and degree of service offered (no-frills, limited, full).

**Step 2:** plot the firms on a **two-variable map** using pairs of these differentiating characteristics. **Step 3:** assign firms that fall in about the same **strategy space** to the same strategic group.
**Step 4:** draw circles around each strategic group, **making the circles proportional to the size of the group's respective share of total industry sales revenues**.

**Insights:** it shows the competitive positioning of firms; identifies **direct competitors within the same strategic group**; reveals **market gaps or opportunities** such as underserved segments; highlights **mobility barriers between groups**, such as the difficulty of moving from the low-end to the premium segment; and assists in analysing the **intensity of competition within and across groups**.

official_questions.question: Riya Sharma owns a confectionery business in Jaipur, specializing in homemade chocolates and candies. Despite holding a substantial market share in the central region, her business has experienced declining sales of these products over the last few years. Concerned about the market dynamics, Riya consults a management expert for guidance. The consultant recommends a comprehensive understanding of the competitive landscape. Explain the steps to be followed by Riya Sharma to understand the competitive landscape to address the sales decline.
answer_points: **(i) Identify the competitor:** the first step is to identify the competitors in the firm's industry and have actual data about their respective market share.

**(ii) Understand the competitors:** once identified, the strategist can use market research reports, the internet, newspapers, social media, industry reports and various other sources to understand the products and services offered by them in different markets.

**(iii) Determine the strengths of the competitors:** what is the strength of the competitors? What do they do well? Do they offer great products? Do they utilise marketing in a way that comparatively reaches out to more consumers? Why do customers give them their business?

**(iv) Determine the weaknesses of the competitors:** weaknesses (and strengths) can be identified by going through consumer reports and reviews appearing in various media — consumers are often willing to give their opinions, especially when the products or services are either great or very poor.

**(v) Put all of the information together:** the strategist should put together all information about competitors and draw inference about what they are not offering and what the firm can do to fill in the gaps; the strategist can also know the areas which need to be strengthened by the firm.

**Note on classification:** although the stem talks about market dynamics and rising competition, ICAI's published answer is the five steps of the competitive landscape, **not** Porter's five forces. The identical case and answer were reprinted two years later as RTP-J26-SQ9.

official_questions.question: Mr. Arun Kumar has built a successful business in the handmade ceramic products industry in Gujarat. However, recent market shifts and rising competition have impacted sales. **(i) Identify the competitor:** gather actual data on the market share and positioning of competitors within the handmade ceramic products industry.

**(ii) Understand the competitors:** use market research reports, the internet, newspapers, social media, industry reports and other sources to understand the products and services offered and how competitors position themselves in different markets, including their unique selling propositions.

**(iii) Determine the strengths of the competitors:** assess what competitors excel at — superior product quality, marketing strategies that reach a wider base, and why consumers choose them — to identify where CeramiCrafts can enhance its offerings.

**(iv) Determine the weaknesses of the competitors:** identify weaknesses by reviewing customer feedback, consumer reports and reviews, and find opportunities to position CeramiCrafts as a better alternative.

**(v) Put all of the information together:** consolidate everything to identify gaps in the market the company can fill and areas where it needs to improve, then devise strategies that strengthen its market position.
